label: text_38
text: That might give Trump the per-fect excuse to avoid his ‘First Buddy’ – as the tycoon calls him-self – although Musk could always ask for something else. After all, while opponents complain he’s

label: text_39
text: Pundits predict that Musk will want to stay as physically close to Trump as possible – which, from January 20, means an office on the White House campus. And if not that, at least have one of the treasured ‘access all areas’ secu-rity passes that Trump used to give out to favoured cronies dur-ing his first term and which would allow Musk to wander around the White House at will.

label: text_40
text: Haberman doesn't believe Musk will get the office or the pass – he has too many enemies and Trump insiders don't want him, of all peo-ple, ‘running around this way’, she says. But at the same time, she acknowledges Trump is tradition-ally slow to dispense with people who have been useful to him and rarely exiles anyone entirely.

label: text_41
text: Indeed, some argue that Trump cannot afford to antagonise Musk. That’s not only because of his vast wealth – and willingness to plough it into politics – or his ownership of the social media platform that remains the most powerful com-munication channel in the US.

label: text_42
text: Nasa needs Musk’s SpaceX rockets to get US equipment and astronauts into space. Having accepted his shilling and let him into the gang, Trump may find Musk – who knows how to bear a grudge just as much as he does – difficult to shrug off. There will certainly be many in Whitehall and other European governments who sincerely hope that Trump does rein him in – and soon.

label: text_43
text: MERICA has becomeincreasingly reliant some say too reliant -on Musk businesses.

label: text_44
text: The 53-year-old, estimated to be worth £340billion, controls the Starlink satellite network which plays a crucial defence role and on which Ukraine’s military depends for internet coverage.

label: text_45
text: Some Washington experts say this is bound to happen. While it may be fine to drop in on the president-elect at Mar-a-Lago, once he’s Leader of the Free World, this becomes a lot harder. Insiders claim that if and when Musk does officially become part of the next Trump administration, he will have to abide by the usual constraints on presidential officials.

label: text_46
text: However, Musk is not great at restraint while Trump is not great at following the rules. And neither man, alike in more ways than just their huge egotism, likes sharing the stage.

label: text_47
text: As Americans head into one of the most unpredictable presiden-cies in living memory, they can at least reassure themselves of one certainty. Born in South Africa to non-US parents, Musk is barred under the Constitution from run-ning for the presidency himself.

label: text_05
text: A NEW year is the prime time to get into healthier habits – including saving for the future.

label: text_06
text: According to financial informationwebsite Moneyfacts, the choice of cashsavings deals on the market reached

label: text_07
text: the highest point inDecember since itsrecords started in 2007.More than 2,000 products were available, sothere's a lot to unpick.

label: text_09
text: Whether you are a seasoned saver or are

label: text_10
text: taking your first steps into the world of investment, Clare Francis, director of savings and investments at Barclays Smart Investor, above, has tips to help grow a handy pot of cash:

label: paragraph_title_11
text: 1Create and stickto a budget

label: text_12
text: “The importance of a well-structured budget really cannot be overstated,” says Clare.

label: text_13
text: She suggests reviewing your monthly income and outgoings to identify areas where you can cut back on non-essential spending.

label: text_14
text: “The money you save can be used to pay off debts, moved into a savings account, or even invested for your future,” Clare adds.

label: text_15
text: “By taking a proactive approach to your budgeting, you not only ensure that every pound is working as hard as possible for you, but that you also cultivate a mindset for long-term financial success.”

label: text_16
text: There are plenty of free budgeting tools available online that could help, such as the budget planner from the government-backed MoneyHelper service at moneyhelper.org.uk.

label: text_17
text: It takes about ’10 minutes to complete and can give you a fresh outlook and new understanding of your cash.

label: paragraph_title_18
text: 2Think about yourfinancial goals

label: text_19
text: “You don’t need to have all your life goals nailed down perfectly, but having a rough idea of what youire aiming for and how much money you’ll need is helpful,” says Clare.

label: text_20
text: “It provides a useful starting point to weigh up the best options available to you.”

label: text_21
text: Many people keep all their cash in savings accounts.

label: text_22
text: But Clare suggests that if you've got money you can afford to put away for the longer term, perhaps for five years or more, then investing could be worth considering.

label: text_23
text: Money held in investments may potentially see stronger growth over the longer-term than savings held in cash.

label: text_24
text: But people putting money into investments will need to be comfort-able with the risks and be aware that they could potentially get less money back than they put in.

label: text_25
text: Analysis by Barclays indi-cates that many savers could be missing out on potentially higher returns.

label: text_26
text: It estimates that 13million UK adults hold £430billion of “possible investments” in cash savings, so they could be missing out on a lot of extra

label: paragraph_title_29
text: 3Consider how hands-on you want to be

label: text_30
text: Choosing where and how to invest money can feel daunting, which may for some people be a barrier to moving some of their money from cash savings into investments.

label: text_31
text: “Many people face a choice paralysis, where they are afraid of making the wrong decision, and it prevents them from taking the next step,” Clare explains.

label: text_33
text: She also highlights the fact many providers offer ready-made investments

label: text_34
text: funds, which may be a good place to start for some people.

label: text_35
text: “These types of funds provide global diversification and invest in a mixture of cash, bonds and shares but the levels of risk vary” explains Clare.

label: text_36
text: “So, all you need to do is to pick a fund with a level of risk that you're comfortable with.”

label: paragraph_title_37
text: 4 Look for financial guidance from reputable sources

label: text_38
text: Clare says: “Our recent research found that a quarter of Brits are now turning to social media, community messaging apps and online forums for information about investing.”

label: text_39
text: Clare suggests that when looking at content from a financial influence, or “finfluence” check out their bio to see

label: text_40
text: if they have a background in finance or experience in the investment field.

label: text_41
text: “If you struggle to reassure yourself that they know what they are talking about, be cautious about acting on their guidance,” she says.

label: text_42
text: She also warns that, with many investment scams starting on social media, it is important to “sense check” any information that is being shared online.

label: text_43
text: Consider whether claims about high investment returns, for example, seem too good to be true.

label: text_44
text: It is crucial to keep in mind as well that fraudsters may use deepfake videos or other bogus information to give the false impression that an investment scheme has been endorsed by celebrities.

label: text_45

label: doc_title_06
text: Suspect stunned to see video of himself torching woman: documents

label: paragraph_title_07
text: BY JOHN ANNESENEW YORK DAILY NEWS

label: text_08
text: Sebastian Zapeta, the migrant accused of fatally setting homeless woman DebrinKawam on fire on a Coney Island subway train, pleaded not guilty Tuesday – even as court papers revealed he said, “Oh, damn, that’s me,” when shown the horrific video of the attack that shocked the city.

label: text_09
text: Zapeta, a 33-year-old Guatemalan mi-grant living in a Brooklyn men’s shelter, was arraigned before Brooklyn Supreme Court Justice Danny Chun on first-degree murder and arson charges. Chun ordered he remain held without bail until his next court appearance March 12.

label: text_10
text: Until recently, 57-year-old Kawam was listed as a “Jane Doe” on the indicment against Zapeta. Authorities identified her last week and Assistant District Attorney Matthew Perry on Tuesday had the docu-ment amended to include her name.

label: text_11
text: After Zapeta’s arrest, he told a trio of NYPD detectives – one of whom translat-ed from Spanish – that he had no memory of what he’d done and that he often drank so much he would “erase the memory” of what happened and wake up at home.

label: text_12
text: The detections confronted him with the video, with one telling him, “The best thing for us here, we want to know why

label: text_13
text: you went to that woman in front of youand set fire to her. Why did you do it?”

label: text_14
text: “To tell you the truth, to be honest, Idon’t remember,” Zapeta replied.

label: text_15
text: When the detectives showed Zapeta video of himself as he lit Kawam ablaze, he responded with surprise, according to court documents.

label: text_16
text: “Who is that person?” the Span-ish-speaking detective asks, and Zapeta responds, “Oh, damn, that’s me.”

label: text_17
text: “That’s you, right?” the cop continues,and Zapeta responds, “Yes.”

label: text_18
text: “Do you see what's happening now?Do you see what you're doing? You aresetting that woman on fire. Do you remember that or not?” the detective asks.

label: text_19
text: “No, I really don’t remember,” Zapeta responds.

label: text_20
text: “But that’s you, right?” the detective asks.

label: text_21
text: “Yes,” Zapeta replies, according to the court documents.

label: text_22
text: When asked again why he did it, Za-peta responds, “I am very sorry. I didn’t mean to. But I really don’t know. I don’t know what happened, but I’m very sorry for that woman.”

label: text_23
text: Zapeta approached Kawam as she slept in an F train stopped at the end of the line at Coney Island-Stillwell Ave. station at about 7:30 a.m. Dec. 22,

label: text_24
text: according to cops. They appeared to be strangers, police said.

label: text_25
text: He said nothing to her as he set her clothing ablaze with a lighter, then fanned the fire with a shirt as the flames engulfed her, according to prosecutors.

label: text_26
text: Chilling video shows Zapeta sitting on a bench on the train platform as Kawam burned to death as she stood helplessly near the subway car’s open door.

label: text_27
text: Surveillance video later recovered by cops shows Zapeta inside the subway car and a police officer’s body cam got a clear shot of his face, cops said. The NYPD quickly released images of the suspect to the media and a trio of high schoolers spotted him on another train later in the day and called 911, the com-missioner said.

label: text_28
text: Zapeta was arrested by Customs andBorder Patrol in Arizona on June 2, 2018,sources said, then removed by Immigra-tion and Customs Enforcement officialsand returned to Guatemala. But he madehis way back to the U.S. sometime after.

label: text_29
text: Zapeta told the detectives he came back to the U.S. illegally about five years ago, arriving in Queens with his wife’s neph-ew. Relatives took him in but that living situation fell apart during the COVID-19 pandemic.

label: text_30
text: “I stayed with them, but in the

label: text_31
text: pandemic, they threw me out because ofmy brother-in-law. Okay, after the pan-demic I went out to work and my brother-in-law called them and told him that... my brother-in-law was working with us, andhe said that all the guys that worked therewere infected with coronavirus.”

label: text_32
text: Up until his arrest, he was doing con-struction work in Queens, meeting his employer, who he refers to as “the Mex-ican,” outside the boss’ house in Jamaica before a job.

label: text_33
text: “He has a lot of work. He takes us to Brooklyn, or in Queens ... or Wall Street,” he told the detections.

label: text_34
text: He finished work the day before the attack about 5:30 p.m., then after his employer picked him up and drove him back to Queens, he went to a bar in Jamaica to buy beer and get drunk, he told detectives.

label: text_35
text: Zapeta had $178.80 on him when police arrested him and told the cops processing him, “That’s all I have.”

label: text_36
text: He had to hand over his sweater and a bracelet and when the officers noted he was wearing two pairs of pants he explained, “I have two because of the cold weather.”

label: text_37
text: His lawyer, Andrew Friedman, once again reserved the right to apply for bail at a later date.

text: BY JAMI GANZNEW YORK DAILY NEWS

label: text_05
text: Scarlett Johansson is making a pivot to hosting daytime TV – at least for the time being, as she temporarily co-hosts the “Today” show following Hoda Kotb’s departure.

label: text_06
text: The 40-year-old two-time Oscar nominee (photo) will guest co-host “Today with Jenna & Friends” for a week later this month, Jenna Bush Hager told People. The Marvel superstar’s gig will kick off Jan. 20.

label: text_07
text: “Scarlett Johansson is the queen! ... We have so much in common,” the 43-year-old day-time show host said of the “wild dream.”

label: text_08
text: The pair’s similarities include being “big reader[s], which will be so much fun,” as well as the fact that both are fraternal twins – Bush Hager with sister Barbara and Johansson with brother Hunt-er. Both are also moms to young daughters.

label: header_09
text: Wednesday, January 8, 2025

label: text_10
text: Bush Hager is mom to 11-year-old Mila. The “Lost in Translation” star, 40, shares daughter Rose, 10, with ex-husband Romain Dauriac.

label: text_11
text: Johansson’s guest stint, while exciting for Bush Hager, is among many “bittersweet” changes com-ing to NBC’s legacy morning show amid her fourth hour co-anchor’s departure.

label: text_12
text: “I adore Hoda. She’s the best partner. She’s been the most gener-ous partner, and we are truly really

label: text_14
text: great friends, so the thought of her not being here is almost too much to bear;” Bush Hager told People.

label: text_15
text: Kotb announced in late Sep-tember that, after five years of co-anchoring “Today,” she would be leaving. Kotb spent a total of 20 years at the show.

label: text_16
text: Referring to her tenure at thenetwork as “the longest profes-sional love affair of my life,” Kotbsaid she “realized it was time forme to turn the page at 60, and totry something new.”

label: text_17
text: Though “a painful” transition, Kotb concluded she was “making the right decision.”

label: text_18
text: Beginning Jan. 10, Craig Melvin will replace Kotb to co-anchor the 7 a.m. to 9 a.m. slot of “Today” alongside Savannah Guthrie. Melvin, who has been at NBC News for over a decade, currently co-anchors the 9 a.m. hour.

label: text_19
text: Upon announcing the news in November, Kotb said that her 45-year-old successor was “literal-ly made for this job.”

text: “The Music Man” co-stars (photo) had dinner in Santa Mon-ica, arriving together and holding hands for a short stroll, People magazine reported. They were spotted smiling, chatting and gen-erally enjoying themselves.

label: text_24
text: Rumors had swirled for months that Jackson, 56, and Foster, 49, were seeing each other after both announced separations from their longtime spouses. The duo had ob-vious chemistry when they starred in the Broadway revival of “The Music Man” in 2022.

label: text_25
text: “The show is so joyful, and I’m having the time of my life playing opposite this guy,” Foster said during a joint appearance on “Late Night With Seth Meyers” in May 2022. “It’s like – it’s a dream come true.”

label: text_26
text: In September 2023, Jack-man and his wife of 27 years,

label: text_28
text: Deborra-Lee Furness, announced plans to separate. At the time, they said they had “decided to separate to pursue our individual growth.”

label: text_29
text: Then, this past October, Fos-ter and her husband of 10 years, screenwriter Ted Griffin, revealed their own plans to divorce. Short-ly afterward, rumors swirled that Jackman and Foster were involved together.

label: text_30
text: “Sutton and Hugh’s relation-ship is the reason Hugh and Debgot divorced,” an unnamed sourcetold Us Weekly in November. “Alot of people on Broadway knew,and we kept it quiet because bothof them are so nice and greatpeople. Everyone respected theirprivacy. But there was an affairand overlap.”

label: text_31
text: Jackman and Foster have not publicly commented on their relationship.

label: text_35
text: BY JOSEPH WILKINSONNEW YORK DAILY NEWS

label: text_36
text: Jennifer Lopez and Ben Affleck have asked a judge to finalize their divorce settlement less than five months after filing to separate.

label: text_37
text: The duo reached the settlement in September through mediation but only got around to filing in court on Monday.

label: text_38
text: The agreement includes no spousal support from either party and says Affleck and Lopez will each keep whatever individual earnings they accrued during the two-year return of Bennifer. Despite their celebrity status, the duo did not have a prenuptial agreement.

label: text_39
text: A Los Angeles Superior Court judge is sched-uled to approve the settlement on Feb. 20, accord-ing to TMZ.

label: text_40
text: Affleck, 52, and Lopez, 55, first started dating in

label: text_41
text: 2002 after they met on the set of “Gigli.” They got engaged at the end of that year, but called off the wedding by January 2004, blaming the pressure of the spotlight.

label: text_42
text: In the following 17 years, both Affleck and Lo-pez had other relationships. But in 2021, they re-united in the public eye once again. By April 2022 they were engaged again, and then in July 2022 they got married at a secret wedding ceremony in Las Vegas.

label: text_43
text: “[Planning] the wedding was so stressful, andone day Ben just says, ‘F− it, let’s just go to Vegasand get married tonight,” Lopez recalled in January2025.

label: text_44
text: But the second time wasn’t meant to be, either. By April 2024, the power couple had started living separate lives, according to their divorce filing. Lopez officially initiated the divorce in August.

text: U.S. says genocide under way in Sudan

label: text_06
text: Secretary of Stateannounces sanctionsagainst RSF commander,and seven companiescontrolled by the militia

label: text_07
text: GEOFREY YORKAFRICA BUREAU CHIEFJOHANNESBURG

label: text_08
text: Sudan’s powerful Rapid SupportForces militia has committedgenocide by systematically perpetrating murder and sexual vio-lence against adults and childrenfrom minority ethnic groups, theUnited States says.

label: text_09
text: The long-awaited genocide declaration had been contemplated by the Joe Biden administration for many months, but it was finally announced on Tues-day as one of the administration’s last acts, less than two weeks be-fore Mr. Biden hands over the presidency to Donald Trump.

label: text_10
text: “The RSF and allied militishave systematically murderedmen and boys – even infants – onan ethnic basis, and deliberatelytargeted women and girls fromcertain ethnic groups for rapeand other forms of brutal sexualviolence,” U.S. Secretary of StateAntony Blinken said in a state-ment.

label: text_11
text: “Those same militias have targeted fleing civilians, nurdering innocent people escaping conflict, and prevented remaining civilians from accessing lifeaving supplies,” he said. “Based on this information, I have now concluded that members of the RSF and allied militias have committed genocide in Sudan.”

label: text_12
text: The Biden administration also announced sanctions against the RSF’s long-time commander, General Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, known as Hemedi, along with seven companies controlled by the RSF in the United Arab Emirates, a wealthy Gulf state that is reportedly supplying weapons to the paramiliary

label: text_13
text: People displaced by conflict in Sudan ride aboard a bus Tuesday to return home to the southern city of Singah in Sennar province, which was retaken by the Sudanese army forces from the Rapid Support Forces in November, 2024. AFP VIA GETTY IMAGES

label: text_14
text: group.

label: text_15
text: Several of the UAE-based com-panies were providing weapons or money to the RSF, while anoth-er was buying gold from the RSF’s mining operations in Sudan, the U.S. Treasury Department said in its sanctions decision.

label: text_16
text: The war in Sudan, which erupt-ed 21 months ago in a power struggle between the RSF and the Sudanese military, has killed tens of thousands and triggered the world’s biggest humanitarian ca-tastrophe. More than 12 million people have been forced from their homes and so million are in dire need of emergency aid.

label: text_17
text: A year ago, Mr. Blinken said the RSF and the Sudanese military had both committed war crimes. But he had delayed his decision on a genocide declaration, report-edly because it could have trig-gered an RSF pullout from cease-fire negotiations, which ultimate-ly failed. He may have calculated that Mr. Trump is unlikely to fo-cus on Sudan in the early months of his presidency, so the genocide declaration and sanctions against Gen. Dagalo will be the last

label: text_18
text: chance for Washington to apply pressure on the RSF for the fore-seable future.

label: text_19
text: Last year, U.S. envoy Tom Per-riello said the Sudan war had killed as many as 150,000 people. His estimate was reinforced by a British study, which found that 61,000 people had died in Khar-toum alone in the first 14 months of the war.

label: text_20
text: Sudan is also the site of the world’s only officially declared famine. Late last month, an expert committee said the famine had expanded to five areas of the country, with more than 630,000 people at risk of starvation and a further five areas likely to fall into famine by May.

label: text_21
text: Tuesday’s announcement is the second time in 21 years that the United States has declared the existence of a genocide in Sudan. The previous declaration, in 2004, focused on the RSF’s predecessor, known as the Janjaweed, which committed widespread attocities in the Darfur region of western Sudan to suppress a re-bellion. Despite the evidence of genocide, the RSF was later

label: text_22
text: brought into Sudan’s government and built a vast arsenal ofweapons and fighters.

label: text_23
text: Human rights groups wel-comed the U.S. announcement. “RSF leader General Hemedi is ultimately responsible for some of the most heinous attracities be-ing committed anywhere in the world today,” said John Prender-gast, co-founder of The Sentry, a U.S.-based watchdog group that focuses on Sudan and South Su-dan.

label: text_24
text: “Without serious measures oflegal and financial accountability,the RSF will continue its ram-page,” he said.

label: text_25
text: The Montreal-based RaoulWallenberg Centre for HumanRights said the sanctions were “asignificant step toward justice.” Itcalled on Canada and other countrites to impose similar sanctionson Gen. Dagalo.

label: text_26
text: Some critics noted that the U.S. announcement came more than eight months after the Wallen-berg Centre had made a similar finding of genocide, based on its own research on the killings in Darfur. Wallenberg Centre legal adviser Mutasim Ali, in a social media post, said the U.S. decision to make the genocide declaration “should have been taken sooner:”

label: text_27
text: Cameron Hudson, an Africa analyst at the U.S.-based Center for Strategic and International Studies, said the U.S. announce-ment was long overdue. In a so-cial media post, Mr. Hudson said the sanctions and genocide decla-ration will make it harder for the RSF to position itself as a legiti-mate political actor in postwar Sudan.

label: text_28
text: In recent days, the RSF has been working on a plan to establish a government in the territory that it controls – mainly Darfur and some sections of Khartoum and east-central Sudan. This government, operating parallel to Sudan’s official government, could pave the way for an unofficial partition of the country, similar to the situation in neighbouring Libya, where two rival governments are operating.

label: text_48
text: There are many worthwhile conventions that enable a good defensive pair to score all the tricks to which they're entitled. Some players ignore these conventions, relying more on institute than science, but this is a dangerous way to play the game.

label: text_49
text: Take the present deal, which features top-notch partnership defence. West leads a club, East winning dummy's queen with the ace. East, diagnosing the lead as a possible singleton, returns the three of clubs, ruffed by West with the deuce.

label: text_50
text: East's return of the three, rather than just any club, is conventional. It says that, as be-tween hearts and diamonds, he would prefer that West lead the lower-ranking suit next. (Had East preferred a heart return, he would have led the eight of clubs to ask for the higher-ranking suit.)

label: text_51
text: Accordingly, West leads the diamond three to East's queen and South's ace. Dealzer plays a trump to dummy's jack and East's ace, and now East has a genuine problem.

label: text_52
text: If he thinks West has another trump, East should return a club; but if he thinks West has no more trumps, his best chance is a dia-mond return. With only his own 13 cards to rely on, East might easily go wrong and hand South the contract. But another con-vention, the trump echo, comes to his rescue.

label: text_53
text: West’s ruff with the two of spades, followed later by the play of the four, denies a holding of three trumps. If West had started with the 6-4-2, for example, he would have ruffed the club at trick two with the four and later played the deuce to indicate possession of a third trump.

label: text_54
text: East therefore returns a dia-mond at trick five, and four spades goes down two. With a club return, South makes the contract.

label: text_07
text: Surplus may have political significance amid Trump’s complains about the trade deficit

label: text_08
text: MARK RENDELL

label: text_09
text: Canada posted its ninth-consecu-tive trade deficit in November, but its trade surplus with the United States grew that month, highlighting a key economic dy-namic that has political implica-tions ahead of Donald Trump’s return to the White House later this month.

label: text_10
text: Canada’s total merchandise trade exports increased 2.2 per cent in November, while imports increased 1.8 per cent, narrowing the country’s trade deficit with the rest of the world to $323-mil-lion from a downwardly revised $544-million the month before, Statistics Canada reported Tues-day.

label: text_11
text: At the same time, the long-standing goods trade surplus with the United States increased to $8.2 \cdot $billion from $6.6 \cdot $billion in October, with exports to the U.S. up 6.8 per cent month-to-month and imports up 4.1 per cent.

label: text_12
text: That monthly trade surplus -the result of Canada exporting more to the United States that it imports - is on the small side, compared to the average in re-

label: text_13
text: cent years. However, it may carry larger political significance than usual, given Mr. Trump’s complaints about the U.S. trade deficit with Canada and his threats of tariffs.

label: text_14
text: The president-elect has promised to slap 25-per-cent tariffs on Canadian imports if Ottawa does not address American concerns about border security. Mr. Trump has also compliated about his country’s merchandise trade deficit with Canada, which has averaged a little over $100-billion anually for the past three years on around $1.1-trillion in annual two-way trade. The trade deficits

label: text_15
text: smaller when services are taken into account.

label: text_16
text: “We lose in trade deficits. We’re losing massive,” Mr. Trump said of trade with Canada in a news conference on Tuesday. “You know, they make 20 per cent of our cars. We don’t need that. I’d rather make them in Detroit. We don’t need their cars. We don’t need their lumber. ... We don’t need their dairy products. We have more than they have. We don’t need anything.”

label: text_17
text: Canada’s trade-oriented economy relies heavily on access tothe U.S. market. It’s the destination for around 75 per cent of Can-

label: text_18
text: adian exports, including $166-bilion worth of oil and gas exports and $85-bilion worth of vehicle and auto parts exports in 2023. High and broad-based tarifts could push Canada into a recession and stunt business investment.

label: text_19
text: “The outlook for Canadian trade in 2025 is cloudy at best,”Toronto-Dominion Bank economist Marc Ercolao wrote in a note to clients. “Our base case is that Canada largely avoids a full-scale implementation of Trump’s tariff plan, given our energy-heavy re-lationship with the U.S. – though we acknowledge that any tariffle-vied against Canada has negative consequences for economic growth.”

label: text_20
text: The increase in overall Cana-dian exports was broad-based in November, with metals and non-metallic ores up to 5 per cent, in-dustrial machinery and parts up 3.8 per cent and aircraft and trans-portation equipment up 6.7 per cent. Energy exports rose 2.2 per cent, with a 4.8-per-cent jump in crude oil exports on stronger prices.

label: text_21
text: Motor-vehicle exports, by contrast, contracted 1.2 per cent in November and remain consider-ably lower than a year ago.

label: text_22
text: Canada’s exports to the U.S. have been helped in recent months by a depreciation in the Canadian dollar against the U.S. dollar, which makes Canadian products more appealing to American buyers.

label: text_23
text: Exports may also be getting a boost as companies try to “front-run” potential tarifts by moving goods across the border pre-emptively. A survey of more than 300 Canadian companies in Decem-ber, conducted by the organiza-tion Canadian Manufacturers & Exporters, found that about one-third are accelerating shipments to the U.S.

label: text_24
text: In volume terms, total exportswere up o,s per cent in November.

label: text_25
text: were up o,s per cent in november. “The third consecutive rise in export volumes in November provides further evidence that the economy was gaining mo-mentum at the end of last year,” Stephen Brown, deputy chief North America economist at Cap-ital Economics, wrote in a note to clients. “US. tariffs could cause the recovery to go into reverse this year, but that threat might provide some further support in the near term if U.S. importers try to front-run the tariffs.”

label: text_26
text: Merchandise exports to countries other than the U.S. de-creased 10.3 per cent in Novem-ber, driven by lower shipments ofgold to Hong Kong and nickel tovorway. Canada’s trade deficitwith countries other than theUnited States widened to $8.5-bil-lion in November from $7.2-bil-lion in October.

label: text_27
text: Service exports, meanwhile, contracted o.2 per cent, leaving the services trade deficit at about$300-million, essentially unchanged from the previous month.

text: Over a 36-year career at CIBC, John Hunkin led the bank's expansion in the U.S. market, and oversaw a lucrative push into financing technology companies. PATTI GOWER/THE GLOBE AND MAIL

label: doc_title_30
text: Former CIBC CEO Hunkin dies at 79

label: text_31
text: ANDREWWILLIS

label: text_32
text: JAMES BRADSHAW

label: text_33
text: Former Canadian ImperialBank of Commerce chief executive officer John Hunkin,who tore down silos in financialservices, died Monday at the ageof 79.

label: text_34
text: Several sources said Mr. Hun-kin died of a heart attack.

label: text_35
text: In a message to CIBC employ-ees, chief executive officer VictorDodig said: “fohn was an inspir-ing leader at our bank, who em-phasized our potential for growthand believed deeply in our abilityto lead.”

label: text_36
text: Over a 36-year career at CIBC, Mr. Hunkin led the bank's expan-sion in the U.S. market and direct-ed the union of investment deal-er Wood Gundy, acquired after the 1087 stock market crash, with CIBC's traditional corporate lend-er.

label: text_37
text: As the bank’s CEO from 1999 to 2005, Mr. Hunkin oversaw a lucra-tive push into financing technol-ogy companies. He also dealt with the fallout from the collapse of Enron Corp., with CIBC paying billions to settle lawsuits filed by investors in the failed energy trader.

label: text_38
text: “John was willing to be innova-tive and creative and made bold moves in the capital markets businesses which are responsible for the strong franchise CIBC has today,” said Richard Venn, a for-mer CIBC executive and founding partner at Further Global Capital Management.

label: text_39
text: Mr. Hunkin grew up in the bank’s culture – his father was CIBC’s head of human resources. Mr. Hunkin joined CIBC in 1969 after earning an undergraduate degree from the University of Ma-nitoba in 1967 and his MBA from York University two years later.

label: text_40
text: to’s St. Michael’s Hospital.

label: text_41
text: He supported York throughout his career, as a member of its board, foundation and business school's advisory council. He also volunteered at downtown Toron-

label: text_42
text: “John was a remarkable personin so many ways,” said MelissaMartin, the chair of the St. Michael’s Hospital Foundation. “Hehad an extraordinary business ca-reer, but beyond that he was amagnificent fundraiser.”

label: text_43
text: In 2011, Mr. Hunkin played a key role in securing a $25-million donation to St. Michael’s from Hong Kong billionaire Li Ka-shing, who had a significant in-vestment in CIBC. Ms. Martin said the donation "ignited the hospital’s research initiatives and elevated our scientists' work to new heights."

label: text_44
text: Mr. Hunkin also supported To-ronto’s Centre for Addiction and Mental Health and the Montreal Museum of Fine Arts Foundation. In 2019, Governor-General Julie Payette awarded him the Order of Canada.

label: text_45
text: Early in his banking career, he moved to London to help open CIBC’s European credit division, new territory for the bank. The pioneering role caught the eye of CIBC executive Don Fullerton, who subsequently became CEO. He tasked Mr. Hunkin and colleague Al Flood with setting a strategy for U.S. expansion. The two bankers moved to New York and built a successful corporate lending team, run by Mr. Flood, who went on to succeed Mr. Ful-lerton as the bank’s CEO and Mr. Hunkin’s predecessor.

label: text_46
text: In the late 1980s, the federal government liberalized financial regulations, allowing banks to own investment dealers. CIBC ac-quired Wood Gundy after the dealer lost much of its capital in the 1987 market crash. Initially, the two cultures clashed.

label: text_47
text: To bridge the gulf, Mr. Hunkin quit his corporate lending job at CIBC, giving up his seniority at the bank, to become head of the investment banking team. Under his leadership, CIBC became the first domestic lender to bring corporate and investment banking under one roof.

label: text_48
text: “John was the first banker to cross the line, to turn his back on his career as a corporate banker and jump into investment dealer, and he did it well,” said David Kassie, head of investment banking at CIBC and former chair and CEO at Canacord Genuity Group Inc. “John excelled at building client relationships and was a really good manager of people.”

label: text_49
text: “Putting an investment dealer and a bank together was unchart-ed territory, but John made it happen, mainly because everyone trusted him,” said Tom Woods, CIBC’s former chief financial officer. “He was not afraid to take risks. CIBC’s electronic banking initiative in the U.S. was years ahead of its time, but ultimately had to be wound up.”

label: text_50
text: In 1999, Mr. Flood retired as CEO, and the CIBC board faced a choice between Mr. Hunkin and head of retail banking Holger Kluge as his successor. When Mr. Hunkin got the nod, Mr. Kluge de-parted.

label: text_51
text: Over the first half of Mr. Hun-kin’s tenure as CEO, CIBC outper-formed rivals, cashing in on in-vestments in client companies such as fibre-optic network Glob-al Crossing Ltd. CIBC became a leader in wealth management by acquiring the retail brokerage network of Merrill Lynch Canada Inc. for $600-million.

label: text_52
text: Mr. Hunkin spent the final years of his banking career dealing with Enron litigation. His successor, Gerry McCaughey, eventually settled the lawsuits for $2.5 billion.

label: text_53
text: Mr. Hunkin retired in 2005, andhe and his wife, Susan Crocker, aformer CIBC executive and CEOof the Healthcare of Ontario Pen-sion Plan, moved to Chester, N.S.That summer, he skippered hisnewly acquired 48-foot yacht inthe biennial Marblehead to Hali-fax Ocean Race, a 360-mile eventfrom Massachusetts to Nova Sco-tia. He and his 12-person crew fin-ished first among Canadian en-transts.

text: Ottawa to release letter clarifying rules on private pay for primary care

label: text_55
text: CHRIS HANNAY

label: text_56
text: Ottawa says it is still working on a long-promised letter clar-ifying the rules around out-of-pocket pay for primary health care services despite political upheaval in the capital, contin-uing months of delays that have created uncertainty for pri-vate provides.

label: text_57
text: An estimated six million Canadians are not connected to a family doctor, and many have turned to alternate health care providers such as wirtual care companies that may charge subscription or membership fees for services that would oth-erwise be covered by public insurance.

label: text_58
text: Nearly two years ago, then-minister of health Jean-YvesDuclos said he was “very concerned” about recent increasesin Canadians paying out-of-pocket for medically necessarycare.

label: text_59
text: He pledged to release an interpretation letter outlining the rules governing nurse practitioners and other non-physical health care providers as they relate to the Canada Health Act, which was passed in \(984\) and only explicitly covers services from physics and in hospitals.

label: text_60
text: In the intervening years, nurse practitioners, pharmacists and other health professionals have been granted new authorities to order tests, prescribe medications and provide other services that would otherwise come from a pri-mary-care physician. But they have been left in a grey area that allows them to operate as both public and private providers in a way physicians are barred from.

label: text_61
text: Mark Holland, the Health Min-ister since July, 2023, has contin-ued to promise legal clarity, but a letter has so far not become realized. On Theseday after Prime Minis-

label: text_63
text: Whenever we have providers that are using out-of-pocket, or private pay options, they are being pulled out of the public system to provide that service.

label: text_64
text: DR. JOSS REMERCANADIAN MEDICALASSOCIATION PRESIDENT

label: text_65
text: ou ruesuay, autor runus runus ter Justin Truddeau’s move to prorogue Parliament and an-nouncentr that he will resign as Liberal Leader once a suc-cessoris determined, Mr. Holland’s office provided few details when contacted by The Globe and Mail.

label: text_66
text: “We hope to have more to say on the upcoming letter soon,” spokesperson Matthew Kronberg said in an e-mail.

label: text_67
text: The delays have caused continued uncertainty for both those calling for more private health care options and those who say it is a drain on the publicly funded system.

label: text_68
text: Brett Belchetz, a Toronto physician and chief executive of-ficer of telemedicine platform Maple, has said such compa-nies are necessary for Canadians who don’t have a family doc-tor.

label: text_69
text: He said he is opposed to the type of user fees that “paywall” access to health care providers who then bill public insurance for their services. However, services that are funded too per centby patients or private insurance should be welcomed, he added.

label: text_70
text: “This is how options like employer-funded virtual care have come to be, which millions of Canadians rely on when they can’t find support in our overburdened public health system,” Dr. Belchetz wrote in a LinkedIn post last year.

label: text_71
text: The Canadian Medical Association has recommended that the federal government ban membership fees, user fees or other sorts of payment for primary-care services covered by public insurance.

label: text_72
text: CMA president Joss Reimer, who is a physician in Manitoba, said the association’stop concern is that the growth of private providers is siphoning professionals away from the publicly funded system. That could lead to worsening work force shortages in the public system, which leads to evenless access to public services, in a negative feedback loop.

label: text_73
text: “Whenever we have providers that are using out-of-pocket, or private pay options, they are being pulled out of the public system to provide that service,” Dr. Reimer said.

label: text_74
text: Ontario Health Minister Sylvia Jones wrote to her federalcounterpart last April recommending that non-physicalhealth care providers be banned from charging fees to pro-vide primary-care services.

label: text_75
text: “I am asking for your department and your government consult and work with provinces and territories on a Canada-wide solution to close this loophole, to guard against unin-tended consqueousces, and probability nonphysicals from charging for publicly funded services,” the letter says.

label: text_76
text: Ema Popovic, spokesperson for Ms. Jones, said Ontario is still waiting on a response from Ottawa to their letter.

An extinction-
level reversal for
truth-seeking

label: text_08
text: ChinaStockholders

label: text_11
text: ocial media has always acted as something of a funhouse mirror to society as a whole. The algorithms and amplifications of an always online existence have helped accentuate the worst parts of our lives, while tucking in and hiding the best. It’s part of why we’re so polarised today.

label: text_12
text: Which is what makes a declaration by one titan of big tech this week so worrying. Less than two weeks before Donald Trump returns to the White House, Meta, the parent company of Facebook, WhatsApp, Instagram and Threads, has made major changes to content moderation, and in doing so appears to align itself with the views of the incoming president.

label: text_13
text: In a bizarre video message posted to his personal

label: text_14
text: Facebook page yesterday, Meta’s chief executive officer, Mark Zuckerberg, announced that the platform is getting rid of its factcheckers. In their place? Mob rule.

label: text_15
text: Zuckerberg has said that the platform, which has more than 3 billion people worldwide logging on to its apps every day, will be adopting an Elon Musk-style community notes format for policing what is and isn’t acceptable speech on its platforms. Starting in the US, the company will be dramatically shifting the Overton window towards whoever can shout the loudest.

label: text_16
text: The Meta CEO all but admitted that the move was politically motivated. “It’s time to get back to our roots around free expression,” he said, confessing that “restrictions on topics like immigration and gender [...] are out of touch with mainstream discourse”. He admitted to past “censorship mistakes” - here, probably meaning the past four years of tamping down political speech while a Democratic president was in office - and said he would “work with President Trump to push back against foreign governments going after American companies to censor more”.

label: text_17
text: The most dog-whistle comment was a throwaway remark that Meta would be moving what remained of its trust and safety and content moderation teams out of liberal California, and its US content moderation would now be based in staunchly Republican Texas.

label: text_18
text: To be completely clear: all businesspeople make shrewd moves to accommodate the changing political weather. But few people’s decisions matter more than Zuckerberg’s. He has found himself, in the past 21 years, a central part of western society. Where Meta goes, the world - both online and offline - follows. And Meta has just decided to take a drastic, dramatic handbrake turn to the right.

label: text_19
text: Don’t believe me - believe the watchdogs. “Meta’s announcement today is a retreat from any sane and

label: text_20
text: safe approach to content moderation,” said the Real Facebook Oversight Board, an independent, self-appointed arbiter of Meta’s moves.

label: text_21
text: Outrage and lies can spread easily on social media, and have only been kept partly in check by platforms’ ability to intervene when things get out of hand. Social networks have always struggled to moderate speech. Those platforms haven’t helped themselves with chronic underinvestment in favour of growing their business at all costs. They have long said effective moderation is an unsolvable issue of scale, but it’s a problem they created with an untrammelled pursuit of scale at all costs.

label: text_22
text: Certainly, policing online discourse is difficult, and certainly, content moderation at the level firms like Meta have been trying to operate has not worked. But forswearing it entirely in favour of community notes is not the answer. Suggesting that it is a rational, evidence-based decision hides the reality: this is an expedient move for a man who this week saw the departure of a self-described “radical” centrist, Nick Clegg, as his global policy chief in favour of a Republican-leaning one. And who also appointed Dana White, the Ultimate Fighting Championship CEO and close Trump ally, to Meta’s board.

label: text_23
text: In many ways, you can’t blame Zuckerberg for bending the knee to Donald Trump. The problem is his decision has huge ramifications. This is an extinction-level event for the idea of objective truth on social media - an organism that was already on life support, but was clinging on in part because Meta was willing to fund independent factchecking organisations in order to try to maintain some element of truthfulness, free from political bias. Night is day. Up is down. Meta is X. Mark Zuckerberg is Elon Musk. Buckle up for a turbulent, vitriolic and fact-free four years online.

text: votes had gone to the Communist party; millions switched to Le Pen, who offered them a world in which immigrants were the cause of their ills, and once they had been expelled - and abortion outlawed, the guillotine restored and the police given drastic powers - all would be well. He was successful in federating a variety of social categories: reactionary Catholics and pagan romantics, skinheads and members of the haute bourgeoisie, unemployed factory workers in the north and well-heeled wine growers in the Midi.

label: text_04
text: Born in the Breton fishing village of La Trinité-sur-Mer, he had the birth name of Jean. He reportedly changed it when he first stood for election. His parents were Jean, a fisherman who died after a mine was caught in his net when his son was 14, and Anne-Marie (nee Hervé), a seamstress.

label: text_05
text: At university in Paris, he studied politics and law, and led a rightwing student group with a reputation for violent and racist behaviour. It was widely thought that the loss of his left eye was the result of a fight, and his account of the circumstances varied over the years. More recently he said it was the result of an accident while he was erecting a marquee for a political meeting.

label: text_06
text: In 1953, he volunteered for military service in Indochina, now Vietnam, enrolling as a parachutist in the Foreign Legion and attending officer training school. Demobilised after two years, at the age of 27 he became his country’s youngest member of parliament as a backer of Pierre Poujade, whose support for small shopkeepers and businessmen, and hostility to tax prefigured elements of Le Pen’s later policies. He soon fell out with Poujade, and in 1956 again enlisted, serving in north Africa. Allegations that he was involved in the torture of Algerian prisoners dogged him for years.

label: text_08
text: Re-elected in 1958, he lost his parliamentary seat in 1962 and spent most of the 1960s engaged in far-right politics and in running a business devoted to the sale of recordings of rightwing political figures. In 1972, he founded the FN, and two years later made his first presidential bid.

label: text_09
text: Le Pen’s circumstances were transformed in 1976 when Hubert Lambert, a wealthy admirer, died and left him a fortune and a mansion in Paris. Lambert was heir to a cement fortune, but was physically frail, with psychological troubles. For years there was controversy over the manner of his death at 42. Members of his family sought to have the will annulled, and eventually the legacy was split with another claimant.

label: text_11
text: Le Pen’s new wealth did not enable him to find enough sponsors to run for president in 1981, but throughout the 198os and 9os elections showed considerable underlying support: 14.3% in the 1988 presidential vote, 15% in 1995;

label: text_14
text: almost 10% in the elections of 1986 and 1998; 15% in 1997 (though only 10% in the 2007 presidentials). Many on the conventional right, though not Chirac, were ready to flirt politically with a man who commanded such support.

label: text_15
text: The first round of the 2002 presidential election marked the high point of Le Pen’s long and turbulent career. In the legislative elections that followed, his candidates scored respectably but won no parliamentary seats. Inevitably, the question of his succession arose, but Le Pen made it clear he planned to continue: with the presidential term reduced to five years, he would be a mere 79 in 2007.

label: text_16
text: Marine was given an enhanced role, to the discontent of some of

label: text_17
text: his older and more traditionally minded supporters. After the defection of his chief lieutenant, Bruno Mégret, in the late 90s, no obvious successors emerged: none of the possible contenders had a fraction of his charisma.

label: text_18
text: Marine took as a priority the task of humanising her father’s image, and began increasingly to take over as his political heir. She set about “de-demonising” the FN, and became an altogether more formidable figure, with Jean-Marie marginalised in the battle for the soul and legacy of their party.

label: text_19
text: In September 2024, father and daughter were among 25 people charged with embezzling funds for fake jobs for European parliament assistants between 2004 and 2016. Jean-Marie’s health had been poor, and he did not appear in court. The verdicts are expected shortly.

label: text_20
text: He married Pierrette Lalanne in 1960, and they had three daughters, Marie-Caroline, Yann and Marine.

label: text_21
text: After an acrimonious divorce in 1987, Pierrette denounced Le Pen, and posed for Playboy when he refused to pay alimony. In 1991 he married Jany (Jeanne-Marie) Paschos. She and his daughters survive him. Stephen Jessel

label: text_26
text: Project manager and consultant committed to improving access to the arts, music and cultural events My wife, Helen Mahoney, who has died aged 45 from breast cancer, was a project manager and consultant. She spent her career engaging with arts charities across the north of England, with a particular focus on improving access to music and cultural events.

label: text_27
text: As well as working with organisations such as Opera North, Drake Music and Live Music Now, Helen also had concern for the people involved in running these projects. In 2022 she completed a master’s in social research at York University, graduating with a distinction. Her dissertation looked at the impact on the arts professionals delivering such schemes, and how they might be better supported.

label: text_28
text: While she loved North Yorkshire, she was acutely aware of the issue of rural isolation. She had moved towards improving opportunities to help cultural industries thrive in the countryside. Helen and I had established our own company – Ryedale Creative – and at the time of her death were looking at a range of feasibility studies focusing on creative rural centres.

label: text_29
text: Helen loved dance and performance, and was constantly dreaming up projects, including running Coquette, a burlesque and cabaret night in York, for a number of years. She also performed in burlesque events across the country, and had an affinity for ballet and Bollywood dancing.

label: text_30
text: Born in Bridgend, south Wales, to Liz (nee Williams), a nursery nurse, and Barry Mahoney, a pilot, Helen went to Porthcawl comprehensive school. She then pursued her love of the written word, studying English at Cardiff University, where she and I met in 1998, becoming a couple in 2002.

label: text_31
text: After graduating with a first in 2001, Helen studied for a postgraduate diploma in arts management at the Royal Welsh College of Music and Drama the following year. In 2005 we moved to Yorkshire, where we made our home in the countryside around Ryedale and the Howardian Hills. She and I married in 2009.

label: text_32
text: Helen is survived by me, our son, Noah, her parents and a sister, Carol. Robin Jackson

text: For many years David Lodge(obituary, 4 January) was anastute member of the literatureadvisory panel of Arts CouncilEngland, which I servedas director of literature.

label: text_37
text: In 1995 Lord (Grey) Gowrie was chairing the Arts Council as a whole. As well as being a former Conservative minister for the arts under Margaret Thatcher, he was a literate man and a poet, but he also fancied himself as the next chairman of the panel. Bringing this about meant the defenestration of Michael Holroyd, the chair at the time, and probably the wisest, most experienced literary adviser in the country.

label: text_04
text: The bold nature of these works - some have commented on their frank configuration and their “difficult brown-ish” palette - belies the challenging environment in which Grewal came to embrace painting. At Brighton’s School of Art, he says, the emphasis was on satire and conceptual justification: people doing bad paintings to make fun of the whole idea. His work, by contrast, was figurative and heavy on metaphor, hinging on the expressive, the poetic, the dreamlike. “I might be too earnest,” he says. “There are different ways of making things and some are never going to be me. I’d much rather look at something that’s going to make me cry than laugh, especially in painting.

label: text_05
text: After graduating, he worked as a cleaner, listening to homoerotic audiobooks while trying to keep his studio practice afloat. Then he did an MA at the Royal Drawing School in London - and everything changed. He is keen to namecheck one tutor, Sarah Pickstone, for encouraging him to push his honesty to the limit. “There was this energy that built up within me,” he says. “It demanded I take the clothes off the figures. There was still a lot of metaphor and symbolism, but now the figures were naked and in nature. From there, I got looser and looser.”

label: text_06
text: He spent a month at Rhode Island School of Design, on a scholarship led by Gwen Strahle, who would talk to him about JMW Turner, Frank Auerbach and Leon Kossoff - artists who were fundamental to Grewal, yet unknown to his many of his peers. It felt like validation. He also discovered compressed charcoal and has not stopped using it since.

label: text_07
text: During Covid, since museums were closed, Grewal tracked down National Gallery catalogues on eBay and used the works they contained as drawing inspiration. He dived into queer cinema, became obsessed with Degas. “I really poured my heart into my practice,” he says. “I was drenched in it.”

label: text_08
text: His studio is everything you could want an artist’s studio to be. Paint pots and spills are everywhere. Books line the window sills and shelves, all within

label: text_10
text: easy reach. When a British Museum curator recently discovered Grewal’s charcoal drawings, she directed him to Georges Seurat. “Before Seurat gets to pointillism, he does this dissolving thing,” says Grewal, opening a nearby book to show me. When I mention Eadweard Muybridge’s studies of movement, he replies “Exactly!” and reaches for book about them.“I have all these clipboards,” he says, lifting one up bearing a fragment of a landscape photograph, ready to be consulted while painting. “I think this is how Jenny Saville works. Like, I want to paint this place which is somewhere I haven’t been, but which reminds me of Cornwall. And I

label: text_11
text: For all his love of charcoal, the Studio Voltaire exhibition will feature only paintings on canvas. The refreshed palette – the brilliant azures, yellows and pinks, not to mention the outsized dimensions of that central piece – will surprise fans as much as they have surprised the artist himself.

label: text_12
text: “My paintings often reflect an emotional state,” he says. “They’re an expression of a history, or a memory - a kind of figuring out. In the past, the dark layers have been directly confusing. They’ve been about hiding things. Those qualities are probably going to be in these new paintings now, but they’re also bathed in this light, which I’m surprised about.” He ascribes this - and a “weird confidence” - to time spent sketching around St Ives in Cornwall, as well as to a recent and wide-ranging trip to India, his first to the country his father comes from.

label: text_13
text: Grewal is often described as a queer figurative painter, with his south Asian heritage frequently added to the mix. None of these are labels he particularly covets. “I’m queer and I’m a figurative painter,” he says. “I don’t really know what else to say. It’s almost like I’m being asked to label myself before I’ve made those personal discoveries myself. I haven’t referenced being south Asian in a formal way in an exhibition - because that’s not yet my experience.”

label: text_14
text: For a long time, it felt important that people knew that he was from London. However, he has begun to wonder if the unspecified locations in his paintings are his way of graphing with feelings of displacement. “That is something that I’m processing,” he says. “It’s lovely having people write about your work - but it’s a funny thing when you’re still trying to figure out why you make it.”

label: text_15
text: He goes on: “In queer figuration, there’s a desire for people to think of adolescence, of nymphs, of idealised youth. There’s a yearning for unattainable beauty, or purity, that a lot of older gay men have. There is nostalgia in my work, but there’s also a darkness and a vulnerability. I’m trying to be as honest and as real as possible.” Jake Grewal: Under the Same Sky is at Studio Voltaire, London, from 15 January until 13 April

label: doc_title_17
text: Captive audiences

label: doc_title_18
text: They were built to instil terror. Now the giant domed prisons of the Netherlands are being reborn as arts hubs - with escape rooms. Charis McGowan reports

label: text_19
text: ne of the architectural features that marks out the skyline of Haarlem, a small Dutch city, is a 37.6m-high dome, crowning a rotunda. You might assume it was built

label: text_20
text: for religious purposes - until you notice the bars covering its 230 windows.

label: text_21
text: Operating as a prison from 1899 until 2016, the Koepelgevangenis (“dome prison”) is one of three panoptic penitentiaries built in the Netherlands. All were shut down in the past decade as part of the country’s drive to reduce its prison population and are now being repurposed as arts venues.

label: text_23
text: Haarlem’s Koepel opened as a cultural hub in 2022, thanks to a grassroots initiative led by the local population. “So many of us Haarlemers had been biking around the dome for years, but no one could go in,” says Jacqueline van de Sande, co-founder of the

label: doc_title_24
text: It used to be that you couldn't leave. Now you won't want to

label: text_25
text: Koepel Foundation,the organisationbehind the building’stransformation.“Weneeded to open it up.”

label: text_26
text: As you step inside, you're immediately struck by the vastness of the open space, bathed in sunlight streaming

label: text_27
text: through the 16 original skylights. A cafe fills the ground floor with chatter. Above, nearly all the former cells are being rented. There’s a podcast studio, art school ateliers and gallery spaces, while the darkened cinema bar offers a more intimate charm.

label: text_28
text: The Koepel’s transformation is a far cry from the design’s dark history. The panopticon dates back to the 170os, first envisioned by British philosopher Jeremy Bentham. Circular prisons with a central guard tower meant prisoners could feel as if they were being watched, without really knowing whether they were or not.

label: text_29
text: Few panopticonic structures were ever built, but the Netherlands has emerged as the unwitting “heartland” of panopticondesign. The three well-preserved structures in Haarlem, Breda and Arnhem were engineered by Dutch architect Johan Frederik Metzelaar and his son Willem Cornelis, in the late 188os.

label: text_30
text: After its closure as a prison, the Koepel was temporarily repurposed to house Syrian refugees while the government sought to sell the building. However, its bleak design, dark atmosphere and staggering heating costs of €400,000 a year made it unappealing. “The

label: text_31
text: state was worried it wouldn't sell,” recalls van de Sande. Determined to find a solution, she called developers, universities, museums and organisations to garner support.

label: text_32
text: The foundation eventually got the cooperation of the Haarlem municipality, allowing them to acquire the €6.5m property and embark on a €25m renovation project. Without modifying the protected structure, they were permitted to put extra windows in each cell, add a cinema and upgrade insulation and heating systems, slashing bills by 90%. It is now undergoing further development with a hotel, student accommodation and an escape room planned.

label: text_33
text: The Arnhem panopticon, acquired by Q Hospitality Group, is currently undergoing reconstruction with plans to transform the dome into a multi-function event space and hotel. Breda, jointly acquired by Being and VDD Project Development, is set to open in 2028. The revamped three-hectare site includes private housing around the dome, with the panopticon transformed into an exhibition space.

label: text_34
text: “It’s a big, open space. Where can you find that in historic city centres?” says Bas van Dam, the founder of Being. “There’s an obligation to give new life to places like this.”

label: text_35
text: They have already spoken to creative partners who might want to use the space, including Belgian festival Tomorrowland. “As a prison, it used to be a space where you didn’t want to be and couldn’t leave. We’re going to turn that around,” says van Dam. “You won’t want to leave.”

label: text_36
text: Back in Haarlem, the refurbishment has generated hundreds of jobs and the building welcomes up to 1,500 visitors daily. Yet if its multi-purpose atmosphere feels uplifting, ventures like prison escape rooms (a feature in both Haarlem and Arnhem) risk trivialising the building’s past.

label: text_37
text: One of the most striking experiences is a historical one, in a tiny cell next to the main entrance. On the wall, panels describe the life of Hannie Schaft, one of the few female armed resistance fighters in the Netherlands. She was caught in March 1945 and imprisoned in the Koepel, before being executed aged 24.

label: text_38
text: Sophie Poldermans, author of a book about Schaft’s life, stresses its importance: “So people are aware, not only of Schaft’s story but the fact it was a prison. You can still feel that energy, even though it is now a much lighter space.” Nonetheless, as a Haarlemer herself, she is thrilled to see the dome gain a new life. “It’s an icon. And it’s beautiful.”

label: doc_title_04
text: Why Trump’s Greenland pitch makes good sense

label: text_05
text: In US hands, the minerals and seaboard of the world’s biggest island would strengthen the West

label: text_06
text: RogerBoyes

label: text_08
text: @ROGERBOYES

label: text_09
text: T f there is still a globe in the Oval Office after January 20, President Trump will no doubt give it a spin and wonder again about the huge, frozen landmass within shooting distance of American cities. Greenland — two million square kilometres of it — is in geopolitical contention again.

label: text_10
text: China craves its rare earthminerals. It imagines the world’sbiggest island becoming part of itsPolar Silk Road, a crucial stopoverfor its vessels as they exploit themelting Arctic ice to boost tradebetween Asia and the West.

label: text_11
text: Trump has an answer to that: he wants to buy the place. Rebuffed by Denmark and Greenlanders in his first term, he is ready for a second go. Donald Trump Jr has just touched down in Greenland to start the ball rolling. Two questions, then. Will he succeed? And what changes if the United States, literally, grows?

label: text_12
text: His first attempt was treated as a joke, an act of flamboyant Trumpian overreach. Greenland's prime minister — it has home rule while remaining part of Denmark, which runs its foreign policy and hands out subsidies — declared the island was not for sale. But Trump understood this as a bargaining manoeuvre and never gave up on the idea. After all, Harry Truman considered buying

label: text_13
text: Greenland after the Second World War as a way of cutting off a potential Soviet attack. The purchase never went ahead but America was allowed to build a network of bases, including Thule, which became a key early missile warning station. That gave both Washington and the Greenlanders a sense of security.

label: text_14
text: The end of the Cold War in the 1990s thinned the American presence. Greenlanders missed the jobs and the dollars but they did not miss the Americans: the thunder of aircraft, the pregnant girls and the occasional scare, such as in January 1968 when a B-52 carrying four hydrogen bombs caught fire and plunged into sea ice just outside

label: paragraph_title_15
text: Understandably, theDanes do not wantto lose face or land

label: text_16
text: Thule. The Danes furiously demanded that all the sunken unexploded bombs and the irradiated ice be packed up and flown back to the US for dismantling. If not, Dennark would shut down the Thule base. The US grudgingly agreed.

label: text_17
text: The world, however, has changed for the US, Denmark and the Greenlanders. Since Trump won the election, China has been flexing its muscles. It has conducted its largest naval exercises in decades, launched the world’s biggest amphibious warship, been accused of sabotaging undersea cables in Asia and Europe and hacking the US Treasury, unveiled four new advanced aircraft, rehearsed a naval blockade near

label: text_18
text: Japanese islands for the first time and intensified espionage activity in the West. The point? To help Beijing negotiate with Trump from a position of strength.

label: text_19
text: To counter this, Trump needs to evolve an approach of his own. The Greenland play, coupled perhaps with attempts to regain control of the sensitive Panama Canal, represents a kind of recognition by Trump that the global climate really is changing the strategic environment. After all, a melting Arctic means easier mining access to nickel and cobalt, essential for batteries. And it will break western dependency on China for the rare metals needed for microchips and sonar systems. That represents a learning process from the days of Trump 1.0.

label: text_20
text: Expanding America might seem like a vanity project — the acquisition of Greenland would be almost as significant as the Louisiana purchase of 1803. It would certainly be a sign of a confident superpower. But if not negotiated with sensitivity, it could put him in the same basket as land-graphing Vladimir Putin’s pursuit of a New Russia.

label: text_21
text: At the moment, he seems to be trusting in his powers of persuasion over Greenland’s puny population of 56,000. An old signpost at Kangerlussuaq airport points to Copenhagen (4 hours 15 minutes’ flying time), North Pole (3 hours and 15 minutes) and New York (4 hours).

label: text_22
text: Trump may bet he can make the whole island more prosperous with US investment; make a shopping weekend in New York as feasible as it became for the Icelandic middle.

label: text_23
text: class. Denmark subsidises Greenland but locals say it comes with too much thinly disguised interference. Above all, there is deep resentment about the colonial haughtiness of the Danes. The latest spat is about forced contraception that was pushed on teenage native Greenlanders in the 1970s by the Danish authorities.

label: text_24
text: Denmark, understandably, does not want to lose face or land. King Frederik has recently adjusted the royal coat of arms to include a much larger polar bear representing Greenland. Islanders regarded this as a bit of trolling.

label: text_25
text: Trump could be placing his bets on an independence referendum being held in April. If the Greenlanders vote for it persuasively, it might open another debate: whether the island, with more power to determine its foreign policy, could in some way affiliate with the US.

label: text_26
text: What a signal to China! Maga made flesh. And yet there will be some around Trump who may caution him that facilitating a split with a Nato ally is not a good look. It is, after all, a longstanding ambition of Putin to rule by splitting the western alliance.

label: text_27
text: A more rational goal for the America-expanders may be to reach an arrangement with Greenland and Denmark that allows the US to use those western Greenland territories closest to the US eastern seaboard as a security cushion. Prosperity for Greenlanders, enhanced security for the US and a partial loss of sovereginty for Denmark offset by the offer of a deeper relationship with Washington. A grand bargain?

label: paragraph_title_29
text: Ignorance of history was bless for Bill, Ted and me

label: text_30
text: ill & Ted's Excellent Adventure is, to my mind, a most bodacious film, which was why I feared showing it to my children. A joy of parenting is introducing your kids to things you love. A sadness is seeing them endure the things you love out of politeness.

label: text_31
text: Had it aged badly? Nervously, I watched their reaction.

label: text_32
text: A primer, for those whose cultural education inexplicitly passed over this 1980s classic: for the sake of the future of the universe, for reasons that really don't matter, the teenage Ted has to pass his school history project. To achieve this, time travellers from the future help him meet key figures from the past — Genghis Khan, Sigmund Freud, Napoleon, Socrates, Joan of Arc.

label: text_33
text: Would my sons consider this conceit — a ludicrous worry, I know — contrived? Worse, as we lament the shallowness of history

label: text_34
text: curriculums, would they understandthe references?

label: text_35
text: I needn't have worried. What I realised was, far from my children not understanding, it was me who hadn't. Nine-year-old me enjoyed the slapstick of Genghis Khan wrecking a sports shop. I hadn't known, however, who Genghis Khan was, even with the narrative exposition. “This is a dude who, 700 years ago, totally ravaged China,” explained Ted, “and who, two hours ago, totally ravaged Oshman's Sporting Goods.”

label: text_36
text: My former self laughed at a short Frenchman cheating at bowling then planning an invasion of Russia. But if you had asked me who Napoleon was? Not a clue.

label: text_38
text: My own children had no such confusion. The reason? Another TV show, Horrible Histories. Thanks to the CBBC series, they have better basic history knowledge than I do today. So do their friends.

label: text_40
text: Imagine if one of Michael Gove's education reforms had produced this level of improvement in subject knowledge. Education ministers would travel from around the world to copy it.

label: text_41
text: Now I hear that Horrible Science is coming to TV. It will be, as Ted would say, most triumphant.

label: paragraph_title_42
text: Clean thinking

label: text_43
text: During my morning shower I might just have resolved, for myself at least, that centuries old philosophical battle; whether or not free will is an illusion.

label: text_44
text: Inside the shower, the world is nice. Outside, it is cold and, in my house, best by children. So,

label: text_45
text: leaving it is hard. What I find interesting — and I have spoken to others who find the same — is that leaving happens utiside of my conscious nought. I turn off the shower and, only a half-second later, do I realise, with regret, that I have done so. I would think I was mad if this didn't accord with some — debated — neuroscience. In the 1980s a scientist named Benjamin Libet asked people to flex a finger. He also asked them to closely watch a clock and remember the time they made the decision to do so. He showed, using

label: text_46
text: probes in their brains, that the motor cortex started preparing for the movement believe the person claimed to have told it to do so. Conscious control was an illusion.

label: text_47
text: Maybe, in our cacophony of thoughts, this is missed. Perhaps it is only with simple decisions, such as switching off a shower or ficking a finger, our brain can glimpse the shocking truth about itself; it is nothing more than chemistry.

label: text_50
text: Lmurmurate. In a damp, grey wetland at a damp, grey dusk, we wait. There is always a moment I think it won’t happen. Then, in small groups, they arrive. Soon there is a boiling blob of thousands, shifting and morphing. It is otherworldly, a fluttering, black collective against skeletal trees. For 20 minutes they dance, then, as one, their wings beat with the noise of a sudden storm and they drop into the reeds to sleep.

label: text_51
text: It feels like the sort of spectacle that happens in remote places frequented by the BBC natural history unit. But this isn't the Serengeti. It's here, every winter, in Theale or Twyford or somewhere near you. And most evenings we go, we're the only ones watching.

label: text_52
text: Matthew Parris is away

label: paragraph_title_54
text: We should recall what prompted the Jay inquiry Harvey Proctor

label: text_55
text: P

label: text_56
text: rofessor Alexis Jay, chair of the Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse (IICSA), declared her dismary vesterday at the

label: text_57
text: “politicisation of child sexual abuse”. While her observation is timely, it begs a fundamental question: where was her criticism of the politicians who relentlessly drove this inquiry into existence for their own ends?

label: text_58
text: The origins of the IICSA are rooted not in impartial concern for justice but in the politically charged fervour whipped up by individuals such as Tom Watson, John Mann and Zac Goldsmith, three figures now elevated to the House of Lords. Each used their position to push falsehoods and fuel a national moral panic under the guise of exposing a so-called “VIP paedophile network”.

label: text_59
text: Watson, in particular, stands out for his questionable use of his parliamentary privilege. He peddled the lies of Carl Beech, a convicted fraudster and paedophile whose lurid claims became the backbone of Operation Midland. Watson’s baseless accusations tarnished the reputations of dedicated public servants including the D-Day hero Lord Bramall, falsely accusing him of heinous crimes such as child abuse.

label: text_60
text: Theresa May, as home secretary, irresponsibly echoed this hysteria by stating in November 2014 that Operation Midland was merely “the tip of the iceberg”. It wasn't even the tip of an ice cube.

label: text_61
text: Let us not forget that the IICSA was a product of political pressure, launched not to investigate grooming gangs nor to address systemic failures but to appease MPs hoping to make political capital by pushing for answers to the fabricated claims of abuse at the hands of VIPs. When Operation Midland collapsed, the inquiry scrambled to pivot its focus elsewhere, including grooming gangs — an area in which its work was neither comprehensive nor free from political undertones.

label: text_62
text: If Jay is genuinely concerned about politicisation, she must confront the uncomfortable reality that her inquiry, too, was born from it. While the IICSA may have brought some clarity, it left key questions unanswered: chiefly, why Pakistani grooming gangs were allowed to operate with impunity for so long.

label: text_63
text: Communities in northern towns and cities deserve justice for the systemic failures that enabled such horrors. Yet these same failures remain largely unexamined. It is time to focus on meaningful reforms as well as focused and truly independent inquiries, not on perpetuating the culture of suspicion and slander that brought about this inquiry in the first place.
