label: doc_title_38
text: Wolfson tidings spell trouble ahead

label: text_39
text: BUSINESS COMMENTARY Alistair Osborne

label: text_40
text: hristmas traditions aren't always fair. Take the one that allows Lord Wolfson of Aspley Guise to parade his festive figures ahead of just about every other retailer. How are the rest supposed to keep up with the Next boss: a best-in-class shopkeeper, who once again has upgraded profits guidance?

label: text_41
text: Typically, Santa delivered for Next: full-price sales up an underlying 5.7 per cent over Wolfson's nine weeks of Noel and enough jingling in the tilts to nudge the full-year profit forecasts another 55 million higher to 11.01 billion pre-tax. As for the shares, they rose 4 per cent to 699.12.

label: text_42
text: So, all's well with the world? Not exactly. Wolfson's seasonal update was crowned in thorns: a looming £67 million jump in wage costs, mainly due to Rachel Reeves' budget, and a warning that the UK economy is in for a “lacklustre” year. As he put it: “We believe that UK growth is likely to slow, as employer tax increases, and their potential impact on prices and employment, begin to filter through into the economy.” As ever with Wolfson, too, he brought some forensics to the subject — the sort seemingly beyond most chief executives, let alone government ministers.

label: text_43
text: The chancellor’s budget raised staff costs in two ways. First by upping the national living wage. Then by lifting the main rate of employers’ national insurance contributions (NICs) to 15 per cent from 13.8 per cent and also lowering the threshold at which the tax kicks in to £5,000 from £9,100. And it’s over the threshold that Wolfson’s analysis is particularly telling.

label: text_44
text: Most employees in Next's 458 UK shops are part-times, working when the stores are busiest. They span mothers with school-age kids, students and people between jobs. And when the tax changes take effect in April it's those people who'll be pricier to employ — £20 million more a vear in Next's case.

label: text_45
text: As Wolfson shows, the impact of the higher living wage and the NIC changes on a part-time worker earning £9,520 a year for a 16-hour week tots up to 13.2 per cent of their wage packet. Contrast a full-time staffer on £60,000 a year: just 4 per cent. As he points out, the lower threshold “creates a disproportionate increase in the cost of part-time work in stores”.

label: text_46
text: In short, Reeves’s budget has the biggest impact on poorer workers, Labour’s typical constituency. As Wolfson explains: “I don’t object to it [the lower threshold] in principle. It’s just the speed and scale at which these changes are coming in that is damaging. I don’t think they were well thought through. It would have been more sensible to phase them in.” Worse, they will “exacerbate” a labour market that was “already softening”. This Christmas Next had 20 per cent fewer vacancies but “25 per cent more people applying”.

label: text_47
text: Next can cope. Wolfson will offset higher staff costs with productivity savings and a 1 per cent rise in prices. But, with consumer spending under pressure, he still sees lower growth this year — full-price sales up 3.5 per cent and profits 3.6 per

label: text_49
text: cent versus 2024-25s 5.5 per centand 10 per cent. True, he's renownedfor downplaying his forecasts, evenif he says: “It's better than thalternative”. Yet, if a retailer aswell-run and financed as Next seestrouble abread, what does that meanfor the rest of the sector? Probablynot the happiest new year.

label: paragraph_title_50
text: A starter for six

label: text_51
text: B eing a self-styled “investor”, “blackjack card counter” and “chess master” are no obvious qualifications for successfully sacking the entire boards of seven UK investment trusts. But, they should at least give Saba Capital's founder boss Boaz Weinstein a decent appreciation of odds. Hence, one thought: surely even he isn't expecting victory at all of them.

label: text_52
text: The biggest clue? That he's nominated one of his sidekicks to the board of no less than six of them. Who he? Well, not Max, Saba's chief happiness officer, a key member of the US hedge fund's seven-strong team, right down to his bow tie, even if he happens to be a dog — but Paul Kazarian, a partner & portfolio manager. As you hardly need one of the under-fire trusts, CQS Natural Resources, to point out: “Membership of six UK-quoted company boards is a case of ‘over-boarding’, which most voting advisory bodies would consider to be a breach of the usual standards of corporate governance.”

label: text_53
text: They would. Lob in Kazarian's existing director or trusteeships at three US-listed companies and he would be quite a busy bee, fitting around to endless board meetings. And that's before you consider just how conflicted he'd be, doing all that while still managing Saba portfolios. As CQS also notes: “Saba's materials state that Paul Kazarian has extensive experience as an investment trust director. In fact, according to Companies House records, it appears he has never acted as a director of a UK investment trust, nor even a UK company of any sort.” Starting out with six would be kind of pushing it. Even Weinstein must know that.

label: paragraph_title_54
text: Reeves in a pickle

label: text_55
text: I wo one's yet hit an iceberg — or any other sort of lettuce. But look at the latest from the gilts market yields on the 30-year have hit a 27-year high, up 0.07 percentage points to 5.24 per cent. Even the mini-budget of Liz Truss and Kwasi Kwarcash failed to hit such heady heights.

label: text_56
text: It leaves Rachel Reeves in a bit of a pickle. With borrowing costs rocketing, she's now tight on fiscal headroom, with all but f1 billion of the f9.9 billion wiped out on Capital Economics estimates. The upshot? She could face, it reckons, the “nasty choice of breaking her fiscal rules or announcing more tax rises and/or spending restrarint at a time when the economy is already weak”. How willing would that be for Reeves and her boss, Starmergeddon?

text: ‘People reallydon’t even knowif Denmark hasany legal right toit,’ Trump said.

label: text_53
text: Trump also said his administration would change the name of the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America. “What a beautiful name, and it’s appropriate,” he said.

label: text_54
text: Ahead of Trump’s newsconference, Trump’s eldestson, Donald Trump Jr., arrivedin Greenland—in a Trump-branded plane. The elderTrump wrote in a social-mediapost, “This is a deal that musthappen. MAGA. MAKEGREENLAND GREAT AGAIN!”

label: text_55
text: The president-elect called into a lunchtime gathering of his son and others in Green-land, saying over a speaker phone, “It’s a very special place. It needs security for it-self, but it also needs security very much for the world.”

label: text_56
text: The younger Trump arrived on Tuesday in Nuuk, Green-land’s capital, with an entou-rage that included conservative activist Charlie Kirk; James Blair, political director of the 2024 campaign and incoming senior White House adviser; and Sergio Gor, who will over-see the White House Office of Presidential Personel.

label: text_57
text: Trump’s national-security team has had preliminary dis-

label: text_58
text: cussions about a process by which Trump would direct the State Department to un-dertake negotiations with the governments of Denmark and Greenland, ac-cording to people close to the

label: text_59
text: transition. That could poten-tially happen through a Com-pacts of Free Association agreement—a financial assis-tance pact similar to what the U.S. currently has with several Pacific Island nations.

label: text_60
text: Trump’s advisers hope to launch potential negotiations once the president-elect takes office, the people said.

label: vision_footnote_62
text: Donald Trump Jr. arrived in Nuuk, Greenland, on Tuesday ahead of his father's news conference.

label: text_63
text: But the Trump administra-tion is likely to pursue a nego-tiation that is more nuanced

label: text_64
text: than a real-estate purchase orsweeping annexation, accord-ing to the people close to thetransition.

label: text_65
text: During his first term, Trump expressed varying lev-els of interest in purchasing Greenland after hearing from his aides about its abundant resources and geopolitical im-portance.

label: text_66
text: When The Wall Street Jour-nal first reported of Trump’s interest in the purchase, Greenland’s Ministry of For-eign Affairs said that the is-land wasn’t on the market.

label: text_67
text: Trump’s Tuesday news con-ference touched on several other topics. On the negotia-tions to release hostages

label: text_68
text: seized in Israel by Hamas mili-tants in Gaza, Trump said, “If they’re not back by the time I get into office, all hell will break out in the Middle East, and it will not be good for Hamas, and it will not be good, frankly, for anyone.” Trump has appointed Steve Witkoff, a real-estate execu-tive and close ally, as his en-voy to the Middle East. On Wednesday, Witkoff is ex-pected to join talks in Doha, Qatar, for a cease-fire in Gaza in exchange for the releases of hostages held by Hamas.

label: text_69
text: Four years after the Jan. 6,2021, attack on the U.S. Capi-tol, the president-elect said heis looking at potential pardons

label: text_70
text: for participants charged in the riot, including those charged with violent offenses. “People that were doing some bad things weren’t prosecuted, and people that didn’t even walk into the building are in jail right now,” he said. “So we’ll be looking at the whole thing, but I’ll be making major pardons.”

label: text_71
text: The president-elect said he is open to pushing his legisla-tive agenda through Congress with either a single large bill or two separate bills, weighing in on an issue that has been a point of debate for lawmakers on Capitol Hill. Trump is ex-pected to visit Capitol Hill on Wednesday.

text: WASHINGTON—Here we go again.

label: text_76
text: The U.S. government is hit-ting the debt limit, triggering a familiar cycle of brinkman-ship, bipartisan negotiation and possible crisis. This round, however, has a few twists.

label: text_77
text: Republicans have the power to raise the debt ceiling by themselves, and they will try to do that in their tax, border, energy and spending-cuts leg-islation that would wrap many of President-elect Donald Trump’s priorities into one bill.

label: text_78

Jodey Arrington (R., Texas), chairman of the House Budget Committee. “And Trump’s committed to it.”

label: text_79
text: If Republicans’ efforts col-lapse, they will need to turn to Democrats to avert a potential government default around the middle of the year, possi-bly setting the stage for more deadline drama. While many Democrats have made clear they won’t sign off on a GOP plan that kicks the debt ceil-ing to the next Congress or next president, they have sig-

label: text_81

Brendan Boyle (D., Pa.). label: text_104
text: Trump, seeing the ceiling on the horizon, asked Con-gress to include a debt-limit increase in an end-of-year spending bill in late 2024, a month before his inaugura-tion. The vast majority of House Republicans voted for a two-year debt-limit suspen-sion, even without spending cuts attached.

label: text_105
text: But enough House Republi-cans objected—joined by Dem-ocrats—to prevent that bill from passing, and the ultimate spending bill lacked a debt-limit increase. Trump asked Congress again to raise or eliminate the debt ceiling be-fore he takes office Jan. 20, but lawmakers haven’t acted.

label: text_107

label: doc_title_06
text: Researchers Dig Into RisksOf Ultra-Processed Foods

label: text_07
text: How packaged products are made could hold answers to why some are more unhealthy

label: text_08
text: By Andrea Petersen

label: text_09
text: A

label: text_10
text: new study is helping to answer a pressing nutrition question: Which ultra-processed foods are harming our health—and which

label: text_11
text: might not be so bad?

label: text_12
text: The problem is the way many packaged foods are made, re-searchers believe. Products such as many frozen pizzas, cereals and chips pack more calories per gram than less-processed foods do. And most ultra-processed foods have combinations of salt, fat, sugar and carbohydrates that aren’t gen-erally found in nature, which can make us crave them. Diets high in packaged foods without those traits—such as canned peaches or refried beans—don’t seem to lead people to overeat and gain weight, at least not as much.

label: text_13
text: Those are the findings so far of a continuing study investigating how ultra-processed food affects our bodies. Scientists presented their interim data at a workshop put on by the National Institutes of Health and the U.S. Food and Drug Administration in December.

label: text_14
text: “There might be a way to create the quote, unquote healthy ultra-processed food that’s still conve-nient,” said Kevin D. Hall, the prin-cipal investigator of the study and a scientist at the NIH, giving an ex-ample of a frozen meal with brown rice, beans and a lot of vegetables.

label: text_15
text: Ultra-processed foods make up about 58% of the calories that U.S. adults and children ages 1 and older consume in a day, according to an analysis of federal data. Foods are generally considered ul-tra-processed if they contain in-gredients that you wouldn’t find in a home kitchen, such as high-fractose corn syrup and emulsifi-ers. Yet many scientists believe not all these foods are equally bad—and some might be reason-ably healthy.

label: text_16
text: Recent studies have linked diets high in ultra-processed foods to in-creased risks of obesity, Type 2 dia-betes, cancer, cardiovascular dis-ease and depression. Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the president-elect’s nominee to lead the Department of Health and Human Services, blames chemicals and additives in food for widespread health problems.

label: paragraph_title_17
text: ‘Energy dense’

label: text_18
text: When companies make, say, an energy bar, they often break down the cellular structure of the raw ingredients and remove the water, Hall said. Getting rid of water makes sense for food safety, Hall said, since moisture promotes the growth of bacteria.

label: text_19
text: The process also makes foods more energy dense—meaning they contain more calories per gram than many minimally processed foods do. In the study, the meals with energy-dense foods had about two calories per gram, compared with about one calorie per gram for the meals with fewer en-ergy-dense foods.

label: text_20
text: In addition, many packaged foods combine fat, sugar, sodium and carbs in ways typically not found in nature. For instance, bagels are usually high in carbs and

label: text_21
text: sodium, muffins are high in fatand sugar, and french fries arehigh in fat and sodium.

label: text_22
text: Researchers call these types of foods “hyperpalatable” and they have a strong effect on our brain’s reward system, said Tera Fazzino, associate director of the Cofrin Lo-gan Center for Addiction Research and Treatment at the University of Kansas. This makes it difficult to

label: paragraph_title_23
text: WHERE TO FINDHEALTHIER OPTIONS

label: text_24
text: Preliminary study results and other research suggest that healthier choices for ultra-processed foods include

label: text_25
text: ▶ Canned peaches

label: text_26
text: ▶ Canned refried beans

label: text_27
text: ▶ Canned fruit cocktail

label: text_28
text: ▶ Jarred salsa

label: text_29
text: ▶ Low-sodium soups

label: text_30
text: ▶ Low-fat flavored yogurt

label: text_31
text: stop eating them, Fazzino said.

label: text_32
text: Many seemingly healthy foodsare hyperpalatable, including manyfull-fat flavored yogurts (high fat,high sugar). Salted nuts are hyper-palatable (high sodium, high fat),but plain, unsalted nuts aren’t.

label: text_33
text: Plain nuts “are good, they are pleasant to consume, but I don’t eat the whole can in one sitting,” Fazzino said.

label: paragraph_title_34
text: The study

label: text_35
text: In the current NIH study, 36 par-ticipants live for a month at a fa-cility where their meals are tightly controlled. They spend each week on one of four dies. They are of-fered about 6,000 calories a day and can eat as much as they like.

label: text_36
text: For one week, they eat mini-mally processed foods such as plain oatmeal with strawberries and walnuts. For the other weeks, they get versions of an ultra-processed diet.

label: text_37
text: In one, the meals are energy dense—such as packaged oatmeal with added protein powder, sugar and cream and sweetened cranber-ries—with most calories coming from hard-to-resist hyperpalatable foods, like honey-roasted peanuts.

label: text_38
text: In a second ultra-processeddiet, meals are energy dense, butfewer calories come from those

label: text_39
text: hard-to-resist foods. The third diet included foods such as scram-bled eggs from a liquid egg prod-uct with spinach, flavored yogurt and packaged oatmeal with fiber powder and heavy cream. Those meals weren’t energy-dense or hard to resist.

label: text_40
text: The diets contain roughly the same amounts of calories, fat, sugar, sodium and fiber.

label: text_41
text: In interim results, which came from 18 people, participants re-ported feeling just as full and sat-isfied on all the diets. But when they were on the energy-dense diet with foods such as honey-roasted peanuts, they ate about 1,000 more calories a day than they did while eating the diet with plain oatmeal with strawber-ries and walnuts.

label: text_42
text: Not all the ultra-processed di-ets had such dramatic calorie dif-ferences. When people were on the ultra-processed diet that was neither energy dense nor hyper-palatable, they consumed only about 170 calories more a day.

label: text_43
text: People gained about 1 pound after a week on the energy-dense and hard-to-resist diet. They lost about a half a pound on the mini-mally processed diet—and also on the one with the liquid-scrambled-egg product.

label: text_44
text: The findings suggest that eat-ing packaged foods doesn’t auto-matically result in overeating or weight gain, as long as you stick to foods such as canned refried beans or fruit cocktail, which are low in calories per gram and don’t have the problematic combina-tions of fat, salt, carbs and sugar.

label: text_45
text: There are other concerns about convenience foods beyond weight gain. Some of the additives that many contain have been linked to health problems.

label: paragraph_title_46
text: What you can do

label: text_47
text: The NIH research isn’t complete. But its findings so far suggest you can choose healthier packaged foods by checking labels and calculating calories per gram. Avoid foods that clock in at two calories per gram or more, such as frozen meatballs, and stick to those that are around one calorie per gram, like low-fat flavored yogurt.

label: text_48
text: Or you can combine foods to di-lute the overall energy density of your meal, Hall said. Instead of eat-ing chicken fingers with mac and cheese, have them with a big salad.

label: text_49
text: To avoid hyperpalatable foods, look for products that are low in sodium, Fazzino says. This can include items such as low-sodium frozen meals and soups, she says.

label: doc_title_51
text: Find Your DigitalPhotos to Organize

label: text_52
text: BY SHARA TIBKEN

label: text_53
text: ort through old photos. It's that to-do list item that keeps getting pushed down to make room for tasks that aren't so overwhelming.

label: text_54
text: Who even knows where all those digital files are? There are tens of thousands of images in your iCloud. And more in your Google and Face-book accounts. And your dusty old hard drives. And even those old photo CDs you got from Walgreens a million years ago.

label: text_55
text: But you've got to start some-where, and now is the time. Plan todownload photo files from wherever they might be stashed. Set up a system—such as a spreadsheet or sticky notes—to keep track of all the places you've checked, advises David Shor, co-founder of Tidy Haus, a home- and digital-organization company based in Fort Worth, Texas.

label: text_56
text: “You want to have a little bit of project management in place so you don’t mess up,” he says.

label: text_57
text: Here's a checklist for making sure you don't miss anything.

label: paragraph_title_58
text: Search your Mac or PC

label: text_59
text:
Search in your what or PCM

Think all your photos are stored in that folder neatly labeled Pictures?

Think again. Odds are high that images are lurking in a Downloads

Folder or other random corners of g your laptop.

label: text_60
text: On a Mac, you can search by kind and select “image” or even specific image file types, including JPEG, TIFF, GIF, PNG, BMP and HEIC. (You can also search for “movie” files.) On Windows, you can search inside the taskbar, and can narrow down your query by specific file types.

label: text_61
text: Download from GoogleIf you use the Google Photos appon your phone or computer, it's easyto download the stored files usingGoogle's Takeout tool.

label: text_62
text: On your computer, open a Google webpage and click your picture in the top right corner. Choose “Man-age Your Google Account,” then se-lect “Data & privacy.” Choose “Download your data,” select what items you want to receive and how you want to receive them (such as a download link). You'll get a zip file you can then open and sift through.

label: text_63
text: If you select Google Drive in the tool, you'll also download all other files you saved there. It might be too much. If you think you have images hiding in Google Drive, skip Takeout and just look around by filtering your search to “Photos & images.”

label: paragraph_title_64
text: CollectiCloudphotos

label: text_66
text: If you have an iPhone, you almost certainly have photos saved in iCloud. You can see and download them by going to iCloud.com/photos and signing in with your Apple ID.

label: text_67
text: You can also find them in the Photos app on your Mac, if you have iCloud photo sharing turned on.

label: paragraph_title_68
text: Check Facebook

label: text_69
text: Many of us have had Facebook ac-counts for over a decade and proba-bly shared photos from old cameras we no longer own.

label: text_70
text: Navigate to Meta’s Accounts Center to download your photos. Choose "Your information and per-missions" from the left toolbar and then select "Download your infor-mation." Choose which account you want to download (for instance, Facebook and/or Instagram), then decide how much data you want— everything available or specific types of information.

label: text_71
text: ▲ Photos are often forgotten onFlickr, Dropbox and other accounts.Make a list to check for them.

label: text_72
text: Photos isn't a download category of its own. You have to select Poststo get images, then choose the timeframe and media quality you wantto download.

label: paragraph_title_73
text: Look at old accounts

label: text_74
text: Did you ever keep photos in Flickr, Shutterfly, Dropbox or a similar storage service? If you haven't logged in lately, those photos may be nurried. so lo in and check.

label: text_75
text: in the case of Shutterfly, if you don't make a purchase every 18 months, your photos will be archived. You can still see them and

label: text_76
text: buy prints, but you can't share or download pho-tos until you make a purchase. Shutterfly-owned Snapfish has the same policy.

label: text_77
text: Flickr limits free accounts to 1,000 items and 50 nonpublic images. If you uploaded more than that back when Flickr was more widely used and had higher free-storage limits, the excess images are probably gone.

label: text_78
text: Hunt through old drives and CDs You probably have an old hard drive, flash drive or stack of CDs and DVDs somewhere with photos from your wedding, the birth of your first child or the birthday of a long-gone loved one.

label: text_79
text: Most laptops today don’t have CD drives—or even the older USB-A ports. You might need to invest in a dongle adapter and an external CD/ DVD drive. Luckily, neither of those will break the bank.

label: text_80
text: In some cases, you might find a dead hard drive or even an old phone or tablet that you can't turn on but you suspect might contain some precious memories. If irre-placeable images are on the line, you may want to visit a tech repair shop.

label: text_81
text: Once you have all your digital photos in one place, backing them up to an external drive or catalog-ing them in your Photos app will be a lot easier. Then you can start wor-rying about all the photo prints you have stuffed in boxes in the attic.

label: text_18
text: Continued from page B1

label: text_19
text: Miller said trucking compa-nies will absorb some of the ex-tra costs from the tolls, but they will have to pass on a portion of the fees to customers such as restaurants and bars that al-ready operate on thin margins.

label: text_20
text: “I have heard a lot of concern about losing customers because of increased rates,” he said.

label: text_21
text: Freight companies and their customers say the charges will pile on costs for cargo that can’t reach its des-tination any other way.

label: text_22
text: “A restaurant’s fish order is not taking the subway from the Bronx to Midtown Manhat-tan,” said Andrew Rigie, execu-tive director of New York City Hospitality Alliance, which represents restaurants, bars and nightclubs.

label: text_23
text: “That truck has to come into the zone and our suppliers have told us this is going to increase their cost of doing busi-ness,” Rigie said.

label: text_24
text: About 120,000 trucks and commercial vehicles enter the city each day, according to the

label: text_25
text: city transportation department.

label: text_26
text: John Luciani, an executive atA. Duie Pyle, a West Chester,Pa.-based trucking company fo-cused on the Northeast thatconsolidates shipments frommultiple customers in a singletrailer, says New York City is al-ready the most difficult and ex-pensive city it operates in.

label: text_27
text: Luciani said that because of traffic, A. Duie Pyle’s drivers there average eight deliveries and pickups a day, compared with an average of 23 daily de-liveries and pickups across the wider region. He said average toll costs per delivery are al-most three times higher in the city than regionwide.

label: text_28
text: “The cost of doing business

label: text_29
text: in NYC is significant,” he said.

label: text_31
text: Carriers say they already have plenty of incentives to deliver overnight.

label: text_32
text: Traffic is lighter and curb space is available. But they say many customers can’t ac-cept overnight deliveries be-cause they don’t have over-night staff or a secure location for unattended deliveries.

label: text_33
text: “It’s just another tax and an-other cost of doing business inthe Big Apple,” Luciani said.

President Biden ap-pointed officials, including Federal Trade Commission Chair Lina Khan, who sought to increase enforcement to levels not seen in decades. label: doc_title_03
text: Blackstone TakesStake in Audit Firm

label: text_04
text: BY MARK MAURER

label: text_05
text: New Mountain Capital is selling its stake in accounting firm Citrin Cooperman to an investor group led by Black-stone, the first flip of an audit firm by a private-equity inves-tor.

label: text_06
text: The deal, which would value Citrin Cooperman at more than $2$ billion, is the latest in a series of stakes that private-equity firms are taking in midsize audit and consult-ing firms in the U.S. Account-ing firms are hungry for more money to pay for technology and talent. Many private-equ-uity funds consider account-ing firms to be low-risk in-vestments that could net a sizable return based in part on recurring revenue streams.

label: text_07
text: The Blackstone-led group would take a more than two-thirds ownership stake in Cit-rin, and Blackstone itself holds an interest in the range of 40% to 45% in the group, peo-ple familiar with the transac-tion said.

label: text_08
text: Citrin Cooperman, a NewYork-based accounting firm, inOctober 2021 sold a majoritystake to New Mountain, whichhas about $55 billion in assetsunder management.

label: text_09
text: Citrin Cooperman has grown significantly in the roughly four years since the

label: text_10
text: sale. The firm reported $351.8 million in revenue in 2021. Its 2024 revenue totaled about $900 million, in part due to acquisitions of smaller firms, people familiar said.

label: text_11
text: Blackstone, which manages about $55 billion in assets, would be one of the largest private-equity firms to have a stake in an accounting firm. A group led by Hellman & Fried-man, which managed $120 bil-lion in assets at the end of 2023, bought a stake in Baker Tilly in June. Blackstone par-ticipated in the debt on that deal, providing $450 million of a $1 billion financing package.

label: text_12
text: The sale allows New Moun-tain to focus on boosting reve-nue at Grant Thornton’s U.S. unit, in which it acquired a stake last May. New Mountain aims to merge Grant Thorn-ton’s nonaudit services in the U.S. and more than 10 other international units over the next five years, primarily in Europe and Asia, a person fa-miliar with the plans said.

label: text_13
text: Regulators say they are concerned about potential conflicts of interest from the accounting profession’s growing ties to private equity, given that an auditor’s objec-tivity is critical to the busi-ness of accounting firms.

label: text_14
text: The Financial Times first reported on the deal.

text: Sixth Street Strikes a DealTo Manage Insurer’s Assets

label: text_17
text: NorthwesternMutual to takeansall minority stakein investment firm

label: text_18
text: By Miriam Gottfried

label: text_19
text: Investment firm Sixth Street is forging a partnership with Northwestern Mutual to manage $13 billion of the in-surer’s assets, executives from the companies said. The money will primarily be in-vested in asset-based finance, a hot area that encompasses a swath of consumer lending, including mortgages, credit-card loans and auto loans.

label: text_20
text: Milwaukee-based North-western Mutual also will take a small minority stake in Sixth Street, bolstering the invest-ment firm’s balance sheet to help it fund growth. The stake is of a similar size to the roughly 10% holding Sixth Street bought back from pri-vate-equity firm TPG last year, according to people familiar with the matter.

label: text_21
text: Wall Street’s big push intoinsurance got under way afterApollo Global Managementbegan managing the assets ofAthene, an insurance com-

label: text_22
text: pany it helped create in the aftermath of the 2008-2009 fi-nancial crisis. Other private-equity firms such as KKR, Blackstone and Brookfield have since bought insurers or struck deals to manage their assets.

label: text_23
text: For many firms, private credit has largely been synonymous with lending to midsize companies, often to finance their buyouts by a private-eq-

label: text_24
text: uity firm. Asmanagers increasingly takein cash from insurance companies, they aremoving deeperinto strategiesaimed at providing betterreturns thanc o r p o r a tebonds while remaining rela-

label: text_25
text: tively low-risk. Insurers invest customers’ premiums with the goal of earning more than they must pay out to policy-holders.

label: text_26
text: Unlike most of the deals done by its publicly traded ri-vals, Sixth Street’s partnership with Northwestern Mutual will happen in phases, with money being invested as the

label: text_27
text: best opportunities arise.

label: text_29
text:
$13B

Amount of Northwestern Mutual's assets involved in the deal

label: text_30
text: “If someone gave me $13 billion and said go invest it to-morrow, I might be able to do it, but I probably wouldn’t be able to do it in the best risk-adjusted-return way,” said Mi-chael Muscolino, a Sixth Street co-founder who leads its financial-services efforts.

label: text_31
text: Based in San Francisco,Sixth Street will manage morethan $100 billion in assets af-

label: text_32
text: ter the North-western Mutual commitment. The firm was founded in 2009 by 10 partners, many of whom had pr e vi o u s ly worked to gether under Chief Executive Alan Waxman at Goldman

label: text_33
text: Sachs. The partners were initially backed by TPG but sepa-rated from it in 2020.

label: text_34
text: Sixth Street built a team of 40 people focused on asset-based finance, hiring Michael Dryden from Credit Suisse in 2022 to lead its expansion. The firm had historically in-vested in asset-based finance in a more opportunistic way,

label: text_35
text: snapping up a portfolio of mortgages in the aftermath of the financial crisis, for exam-ple. Now it is investing more consistently as banks have scaled back in response to regulatory pressure.

label: text_36
text: Dryden’s group last month announced a deal to buy as much as $4 billion of loans from buy-now-pay-later plat-form Affirm.

label: text_37
text: Sixth Street has a separate team of 25 people solely fo-cused on insurance. It owns and advises on the invest-ments for Talcott Financial Group, an annuities company with $127 billion in assets.

label: text_38
text: Northwestern Mutual isowned by its policyholders.The company, which wasfounded more than 165 yearsago, provides life, disability-income and long-term-care in-surance, annuities, and bro-kerage and wealth advisory. Itmanages the bulk of its $627billion in assets internally andhas invested in private mar-kets for decades.

label: text_39
text: But Northwestern Mutual didn’t have the capability of finding and structuring asset-based finance deals, a labor-intensive process, according to Jeb Bentley, its chief invest-ment officer.

label: doc_title_40
text: CFTC Chairman to Step Down When Trump Takes Office

label: text_41
text: BY MENGQI SUN

label: text_42
text: Commodity Futures Trad-ing Commission ChairmanRostin Behnam said he wouldstep down from his positionon Jan. 20, as the country’stop derivatives markets regu-lator prepares for a secondTrump term.

label: text_43
text: Behnam, a Democrat, has served as the CFTC’s chairman since 2022. He previously served as a commissioner be-

label: text_44
text: tween 2017 and 2021 and was named acting chairman in 2021 after his predecessor, Heath Tarbert, resigned when President Biden took office.

label: text_45
text: Behnam said that under his leadership, the CFTC shifted its focus from implementing the 2010 Dodd-Frank Act to adapting its oversight respon-sibilities to address the new issues brought on by evolving technology in the derivatives markets and to tackle regula-

label: text_46
text: tory gaps.

label: text_47
text: Behnam has sought a lead-ing role for the CFTC in regu-lating the cryptocurrency market, which has defied easy categorization within the fi-nancial regulatory system. That has put the derivatives regulator in a potential con-flict with the Securities and Exchange Commission around jurisdictional power over the nascent industry.

label: text_48
text: The CFTC has cracked

label: text_49
text: down on misconduct and fraud related to cryptocur-rency over the past few years, suing some of the highest-pro-file companies in the industry. The regulator in August ob-tained $12.7 billion in a judg-ment against now-bankrupt crypto exchange FTX and crypto trading firm Alameda Research. The CFTC also sued crypto exchange Binance for evading U.S. rules in 2023 and imposed a $2.7 billion fine on

label: text_50
text: the company later that year. When a group of regulators announced the deal with Bi-nance at the time, Behnam joined Attorney General Mer-rick Garland and Treasury Secretary Janet Yellen on the stage.

label: text_51
text: Behnam said his last day at the agency will be Feb. 7, add-ing that he would work closely with President-elect Donald Trump’s team to ensure a smooth transition.

label: doc_title_07
text: Strong earthquake hits remote Tibet

label: doc_title_09
text: Dozens killed as cold complicates rescue efforts

label: text_10
text: By David Pierson,Berry Wang,

label: text_11
text: and Bhadra SharmaNEW YORK TIMES

label: text_12
text: HONG KONG — Using their hands and shovels in frigid con-ditions, rescue workers dug through the rubble in the search for survivors after a deadly 7.1 magnitude earth-quake toppled houses and jolt-ed people awake in a remote part of Tibet on Tuesday near the northern foothills of Mount Everest.

label: text_13
text: At least 126 people have died and 188 were injured in the quake, which struck shortly after 9 a.m. at a depth of 6.2 miles in Dingri County, near one of Tibet’s most historic cit-ies, in western China, state me-dia reported. The quake was the country’s deadliest since December 2023, when 151 peo-ple were killed in a 6.2 magni-tude templor in the northwest-ern provinces of Gansu and Qinghai.

label: text_14
text: China’s state broadcaster re-ported that more than 1,000 houses had experienced some form of damage in Dingri County, where the average alti-tude is around 15,000 feet, along the Himalayan border with Nepal.

label: text_15
text: Frantic rescue efforts were being conducted without heavy equipment, underscoring the challenge of delivering resource-es to the largely isolated com-munities damaged by the quake. With temperatures in the region dipping as low as 5 degrees Fahrenheit, rescue workers have a short window in which to locate survivors. It was not immediately clear how many residents had been left homeless.

label: text_16
text: Several aftershocks were felt in the area, including in Nepal. The quake had a magnitude of 7.1, according to the US Geo-logical Survey, though it was measured as 6.8 by the China Earthquake Networks Center.

label: text_17
text: The nearest city to the earth-quake’s epicenter was Shigatse, the second-largest city in Tibet,

label: text_18
text: with a population of 640,000. Shigatse is home to the vast, centuries-old Tashilhunpo Monastery, the traditional seat of the Panchen Lama, one of the most senior figures in Ti-betan Buddhism. State media said no damage to the monas-tery had been reported so far.

label: text_20
text: Scenes of destruction were broadcast on state media and shared on social media. A tour-ist not far from Shigatse who spoke to The New York Times

label: text_21
text: said she was in her hotel room when the earthquake started shaking her building. She said the electricity went out and that she and a friend had squat-ted between the beds. When the shaking stopped, they ran out of the building.

label: text_22
text: The tourist, who only gave her surname, Xu, shared a vid-eo showing several single-story brick buildings with collapsed walls. Video posted on Chinese social media showed streets strewed with rubble, cars crushed by fallen bricks, and roads split open by the shifted ground. Xu said she grabbed her down jacket before she ran out.

label: text_23
text: China’s top leader, Xi Jin-ping, ordered officials to mini-mize casualties and resettle sur-vivors. Chinese authorities de-ployed 3,400 resources and more than 340 medical workers for the search effort, and dis-

label: text_24
text: patched tents, folding beds, winter coats, and quilts, state media reported.

label: text_25
text: Rescue efforts could be af-fected by bottlenecks caused by damaged roads, said Robert Barnett, a professor from SOAS University of London, who has visited the region and de-scribed it as looking like “vastmoonscape.”

label: text_26
text: “This is harsh, high-altitudeland,” Barnett said. “The roadsare quite few and susceptible tolandsides.”

label: text_27
text: That said, Barnett added that there could be new roads connecting some of Dingri County’s most remote border villages built in recent years to assert China’s sovereignty along its periphery.

label: text_28
text: The Himalayan region is prone to powerful earthquakes. In 2015, a quake in Nepal with a magnitude of 7.8 killed nearly 9,000 people. In Kathmandu,

label: text_29
text: Nepal’s capital, residentsstreamed out of their homes inthe morning as the earthquakerattled buildings.

label: text_30
text: At least two people, one in Kathmandu and another one in Sindhupalchowk, a distinct north of Kathmandu, sustained minor injuries from the quake, according to Nepalese police.

label: text_31
text: Nepal sent more than 2,500 police officers to assess damage and look for victims.

label: text_32
text: “Based on the magnitude of the earthquake, there could be some damage in mountains of eastern Nepal,” said Lok Bijaya Adhikari, a senior seismologist at Nepal’s National Earthquake Monitoring and Research Cen-ter.

label: text_33
text: Most residents from Nepal’shigh mountain regions such asEverest, Makalu, Rolwaling,and Kanchenjunga have mi-grated to lowland areas to avoidthe extreme cold of winter.

label: doc_title_34
text: Israeli strikes kill at least 17 people in Gaza Strip

label: vision_footnote_36
text: BASHAR TALEB/AFP VIA GETTY IMAGES

label: vision_footnote_37
text: Rescuers and civilians evacuated a victim of an Israeli strike on a house in Khan Yunis, inthe southern Gaza Strip, on Tuesday.

label: text_38
text: Most women,children despitetargeting Hamas

label: text_39
text: ASSOCIATED PRESS

label: text_40
text: Israeli airstrikes in south-ern Gaza killed at least 17 peo-ple late Tuesday, nearly all of them women or children, the territory’s Health Ministry and hospital officials said.

label: text_41
text: Five children were killed as they sheltered together in the same tent, said Ahmed al-Far-ra, director of the children’s ward at nearby Nasser Hospi-tal in Khan Younis. Their bod-ies were among the eight chil-dren and five women brought to the hospital after strikes on tents, homes, and a vehicle. Two bodies were unidentifi-able.

label: text_42
text: The Israeli military said it targeted militants who had taken part in the Oct. 7, 2023, attack that sparked the war, without providing evidence. Is-rael said it took steps to lessen the risk of hurting civilians and blamed Hamas for the civilian casualties.

label: text_43
text: The Israel-Hamas war in Gaza is raging with no end in sight, although there has re-portedly been recent progress in long-running talks aimed at a cease-fire and the release of Israeli hostages held by Hamas.

label: text_44
text: Displaced Palestinians in the Gaza Strip still have hope that Israel’s 15-month war with Hamas will end soon.

label: text_45
text: “What we are living is not a life. Nobody could bear the situation we’re experiencing for a single day,” said Munawar al-Bik, a displaced woman from Gaza City.

label: text_46
text: “We wake up at night to the sounds of men crying, because of the bad situation,” al-Bik said. “The situation is unbear-able, we have no energy left, we want it to end today.”

label: text_47
text: She spoke to the Associated Press on a dusty road in the southern city of Khan Younis beside the rubble of a de-stroyed building. Behind her, a sea of makeshift tents filled with displaced families stretched into the distance.

label: text_48
text: Muhammad Zaqout, a dis-placed man from Gaza City, said he’s sick of children being killed daily, of the destruction and displacement.

label: text_49
text: In recent months, families who fled their homes in Gaza have had little access to clean water or enough food to eat.

label: text_50
text: and they struggle to cope with harsh winter conditions that have killed several babies from hypothermia in recent weeks.

label: text_51
text: Meanwhile, the Biden ad-ministration in its final days is shifting more than $100$ mil-lion in military aid from Israel and Egypt to Lebanon as it tries to bolster a cease-fire agreement it helped mediate between Israel and Hezbollah.

label: text_52
text: In separate notices sent to Congress, the State Depart-ment said it was moving $95 million in military assistance intended for Egypt and $7.5 million for Israel toward sup-porting the Lebanese army and its government. The notices were dated Jan. 3 and obtained by the Associated Press on Tuesday.

label: text_53
text: Most of the money will go to the Lebanese Armed Forces, which have a critical role in standing up the cease-fire that was agreed to in November fol-lowing an all-out war between Israeli and Hezbollah that bat-tered much of southern and eastern Lebanon for two months.

label: text_54
text: It is intended to help the LAF deploy in the south of the country and supplement the role of the UN peacekeeping mission patrolling the so-called Blue Line, which has separated Israel and Lebanon since the end of a monthlong Israel-Hez-bollah war in 2006.

label: text_55
text: Both Israel and Hezbollah agreed to pull their forces out of southern Lebanon before the end of January, with com-

label: text_56
text: pliance to be overseen by theLebanese army and UN peace-keepers.

label: text_57
text: “US security assistance to the LAF increases its capacity as the country’s only legitimate military force and defender of Lebanon’s territorial integrity, enables the LAF to prevent po-tential destabilization from ISIS and other terrorist groups, and enables the LAF to provide security both for the Lebanese people and for US personnel,” the State Department said.

label: text_58
text: Pro-Israel members of Con-gress and others have in the past complained about any di-version of US assistance to Is-rael, although it was not imme-diately clear if there would be objections to such a small amount of shifted money.

label: text_59
text: At the same time, some of those who have been forceful advocates of Israel and critics of US assistance to the Leba-nese military have often com-plained that it has been infil-trated by Hezbollah. The notic-es rejected that claim.

label: text_60
text: “US support to the LAF re-inforces the LAF as an impor-tant institutional counter-weight to Hezbollah, which re-ceives weapons, training, and financial support from Iran,” the State Department said. “The LAF continues to be an independent, non-sectarian in-stitution in Lebanon, and is re-spected across all sectors.”

label: text_61
text: In a third notice, also sent to Congress on Jan. 3, the de-partment said it was going to provide $15 million to Leba-non’s Internal Security Forces to ensure that they become the primary law enforcement enti-ty in the country and assist the LAF in controlling areas in the south.

label: paragraph_title_63
text: France marks10th anniversaryof terror attack

label: text_64
text: PARIS — A decade after Islamic terrorists stormed the offices of the satirical newspaper Charlie Hebdo in a deadly assault that shook France to its core and ignited a global outcry in defense of freedom of speech, the nation paused on Tuesday to honor the victims and renew its resolve to fight for liberty and democracy.

label: text_65
text: President Emmanuel Ma-cron and Paris Mayor Anne Hi-dalgo led solemn tributes at the site of the attack, where 12 peo-ple, including some of France’s most beloved cartoonists, were killed on Jan. 7, 2015.

label: text_66
text: Among those remembered was Ahmed Merabet, a police officer who was gunned down on the street while defending the newspaper.

label: text_67
text: In a poignant ceremony, Macron stood with his wife, Brigitte, alongside former president François Hollande, who had steered France through the aftermath of the attack. Macron joined police officers in laying wreaths of flowers against the wall of the former Charlie Heb-do headquarters in the 11th distinct and the gathering ob-served a minute of silence.

label: paragraph_title_69
text: Nine workers trapped in mine in northern India

label: text_70
text: GUWAHATI, India — At least nine workers are trapped inside a flooded coal mine in India’s northeastern Assam state, officials said Tuesday, as authorities summoned the army to help in the rescue operation.

label: text_71
text: The miners became trapped on Monday morning in the Um-rangso area in Dima Hasao dis-trict, about 125 miles south of the state capital, Guwahati.

label: text_72
text: The workers are feared trapped 300 feet below the ground after water gushed in from a nearby unused mine.

label: text_73
text: “We are mobilizing resourcesto rescue them,” said KaushikRai, a government minister.

label: text_74
text: Army soldiers and a disaster team used ropes and cranes in the operation. Researchers found three helmets, some slippers, and a few other items, Rai said.

label: text_75
text: “The divers have been able to dive into 35 or 40 feet of water inside the mine,” he said. “The water level now is estimated at 100 feet.”

label: text_76
text: Assam Chief Minister Him-anta Biswa Sarma said that the mine appeared to be illegal, and that police had arrested one per-son thus far.

label: paragraph_title_78
text: S. Korea courtissues new arrestwarrant for Yoon

label: text_79
text: SEOUL — South Korea’s anticorruption agency said it received a new court warrant on Tuesday to detain impeached President Yoon Suk Yeol after its previous attempt was blocked by the presidential security service last week.

label: text_80
text: The Corruption Investigation Office for High-Ranking Offic-cials, which plans to question the embattled president on re-bellion allegations over his short-lived martial law decree on Dec. 3, didn’t confirm how long the warrant would remain valid. Chief prosecutor Oh Dong-woon refused to answer when asked by lawmakers when the warrant would expire, say-ing the information is sensitive.

label: text_81
text: Detention warrants typically last seven days but can be ex-tended to around 10 days. Oh didn’t say when investigators planned to make their next at-tempt to detain Yoon.

label: text_82
text: The Seoul Western District Court last week had initially is-sued a warrant to detain Yoon and a separate warrant to search his residence after he repeatedly defied authorities by refusing to appear for questioning.

text: Norovirus cases in Mass. surged in 2024

label: doc_title_07
text: Officials say 66% jump in a year reflects US trend; call handwashing best defense

label: text_08
text: By Camilo FonsecaGLOBE STAFF

label: text_09
text: Mirroring a national trend, cases of the norovirus stomach bug are surging in Massachusetts this win-ter, according to state data.

label: text_10
text: The state reported 2,080 labora-tory-confirmed cases of the virus in 2024 in preliminary data released last week by the Massachusetts De-partment of Public Health. That represents a jump of roughly 66 percent from the previous year, when the state reported 1,252 cas-es.

label: text_11
text: Cases over the winter have so far outpaced the previous year, with 134 cases reported in November and 279 reported in December. In 2023, there were 52 cases reported in November and 112 in December.

label: text_12
text: Public health officials say they have been monitoring the increase in cases.

label: text_13
text: Nationally, cases of the virus are surging in parts of the United States this winter, according to govern-ment data.

label: text_14
text: The most recent numbers from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention show there were 91 out-breaks of norovirus reported during the week of Dec. 5, up from 69 out-breaks the last week of November.

label: text_15
text: Numbers from the past few years show a maximum of 65 outbreaks reported during that first week of December.

label: text_16
text: Norovirus symptoms include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and ab-dominal cramps, according to state health officials. Despite being one of the most common causes of food-borne illness, the virus is difficult to detect in a laboratory, and special-ized norovirus tests are usually con-ducted only in certain circumstanc-es.

label: text_17
text: A spokesperson for the DPH said the uptick in cases may be attribut-ed in part to more modern testing methods which can detect multiple pathogens at once. They also noted that certain test devices were re-cently found to be prone to false

label: text_18
text: positives of norovirus.

label: text_19
text: Illness caused by norovirus typi-cally starts suddenly, with symp-toms developing 12 to 48 hours fol-lowing exposure to the virus. Most people get better within one to three days and recover fully.

label: text_20
text: People of all ages can get infect-ed and fall sick from norovirus. Young children, older people, and those with weakened immune sys-tems are most at risk, with dehydra-tion from vomiting and diarrhea the top concern.

label: text_21
text: There is no medication to treat norovirus. Rehydration is recom-mended by drinking water and oth-er liquids, with the exception of cof-fee, tea, and alcohol.

label: text_22
text: Health officials also recommend NOROVIRUS, Page B3

text: Boston traffic ranked fourth worst in nation

label: doc_title_28
text: Study finds drivers here spent an average 79 hours stuck in traffic last year

label: paragraph_title_29
text: By Shannon LarsonGLOBE STAFF

label: text_30
text: In what will come as no surprise to any Boston driver: We’re still stuck in traffic. The city continues to rank in the top-five most con-gested cities in the United States and among the worst worldwide.

label: text_31
text: Still, Boston traffic is generally improving. Unless, that is, you’re heading south on I-93 after work.

label: text_32
text: The average motorist traversing Boston spent 79 hours stuck in traf-fic in 2024, according to an annual study from INRIX, a transportation analytics company. In 2023, that av-erage driver lost 88 hours.

label: text_33
text: That 10 percent drop is the larg-est for any of the top 25 most con-gested American cities.

label: text_34
text: Some key factors, according to the Mass. Department of Transportation, include investments in infra-structure, such as optimized traffic signals and dedicated bus lines; public transit enhancements; more people choosing biking or walking; and folks adjusting their commut-ing schedules.

label: text_35
text: “We’re encouraged by this progr-ress, but know there’s still work to be done,” said the state highway ad-ministrator, Jonathan Gulliver.

label: text_36
text: Worldwide, congestion againedged closer to pre-pandemic levelsas more than half of the urban ar-

label: text_37
text: eas studied experienced an increase in traffic — a trend driven, in part, by workers returning to the office. Istanbul, Mexico City, London, and Paris were among the most congest-ed cities, according to the study.

label: text_38
text: In the US last year, the average worker lost 43 hours to traffic jams, the equivalent of a work week, IN-RIX found.

label: text_39
text: “Traffic can be an indicator of economic boon, but ironically, it’s a hamper on economies in of itself. Each minute spent waiting in traf-fic results in money and productivi-ty lost,” said Bob Pishue, transpor-

label: text_40
text: tation analyst at INRIX and authorof the report, which determinedthat $74$ billion was lost to conges-tion nationwide.

label: text_41
text: For another year running, New York was the most congested city in the US, according to the scorecard, with the average New York com-muter losing 102 hours, followed by Chicago drivers who also lost 102 hours, and Los Angeles motorists, who lost 88 hours. People behind the wheel in Boston came in fourth nationwide, the same position it was ranked by INRIX in 2023.

label: doc_title_43
text: Population rise in Mass. is largest in 60 years

label: doc_title_44
text: Census figures show increase largely driven by influx of immigrants

label: paragraph_title_45
text: By Sam DrysdaleSTATE HOUSE NEWS

label: text_46
text: Fueled by the highest immigration levels in decades, Massachusetts saw its largest popula-tion increase in 60 years between 2023 and 2024, and the rate of domestic outmigration has signifi-cantly slowed, according to US Census data re-leased last month.

label: text_47
text: Between July 1, 2023 and July 1, 2024, the state’s population increased 69,603 from 7,066,568 to 7,136,171 – an increase of just un-der 1 percent (0.985 percent).

label: text_48
text: That’s the largest annual percentage increase that Massachusetts has experienced since be-tween 2012 and 2013, according to a UMass Do-nahue Institute analysis of the December US Cen-sus population estimates.

label: text_49
text: Numbers-wise, it’s the largest annual popula-tion increase since the end of the baby boom in 1964.

label: text_50
text: Those gains made Massa-chusetts the fastest growing state in New England and the second-fastest growing state in the Northeast after New Jersey, according to the institute.

label: text_51
text:

label: text_52
text: The largest driver: immi-gration, estimated at 90,217 incoming immigrants be-tween 2023 and 2024. The

label: text_53
text: census estimates that’s the highest immigration level since at least 1990.

label: text_54
text: “While immigration is the single largest driver of population change in Massachusetts ... other factors also play a role,” according to the insti-tute’s analysis. “In 2024, Massachusetts saw more births (67,851) than deaths (61,133), contribut-ing 6,718, on net, to the population growth in Massachusetts.”

label: text_55
text: Massachusetts has seen an influx of thousands of refugees and migrants — seeking asylum from wars, political unrest, and environmental disas-ters — who have sought temporary housing in the state’s emergency family shelter system, straining the physical and financial limits of the system. The census data does not delineate between im-migrants legally seeking asylum or refuge and those otherwise entering the country.

text: Brown professor conducted groundbreaking research into eating disorders and obesity

label: text_66
text: By Bryan MarquardGLOBE STAFF

label: text_67
text: Alison Field traced her early insights into obesity and eating disorders to a job in the late 1980s that seemed far removed from the international reputation she would earn as a professor and researcher.

label: text_68
text: While attending college in California, she was a consultant to a Jenny Craig weight loss clinic and began honing skills she would bring to decades of studies: listening to those trying to lose weight, and watching carefully and compassionately to see how nuanced differences among people could splinter a sweep-ing diagnosis into subcategories.

label: text_69
text: “There probably isn’t one magic bullet for obesity,” Dr. Field said in 2018, when she was lead author of a paper published in the journal Obesity that analyzed data from more than 2,400 patients who had undergone bariatric weight-loss surgery.

label: text_70
text: “If there is a magic bullet,” she added, “it’s going to be differ-ent for different groups of people.”

label: text_71
text: Dr. Field, an epidemiology professor and associate dean for faculty affairs at the Brown University School of Public Healthwho formerly taught at Harvard Medical School, died Oct. 10 inher home in the Newton section of Chestnut Hill.

label: doc_title_09
text: Doherty's special path

label: paragraph_title_10
text: Hingham captain shows MIAA way to college play

label: paragraph_title_11
text: By Mike PuzzangheragLOBE CORRESPONDENT

label: text_12
text: Caroline Doherty is evidence that there’s no set path to a dream.

label: text_13
text: Hingham’s star senior forward — committed to play at Holy Cross after a post-grad year — has done it all while playing for the town she grew up in. She’s the school’s all-time leading scorer, a two-time Patriot League MVP, and one of the state’s most talented players.

label: text_14
text: She takes immense pride in the career she’s built at Hingham.

label: text_15
text: “Personally, I don’t think it matters where you go to school, as long as you put the work in,” Do-herty said. “I get to play with my sister [Brenna] and all the people I grew up playing with. I think the ‘public pride’ part of it is honestly my favorite part.

label: text_16
text: “I play in front of the little girls who all look up to all of us. That’s probably the best part of it, too.”

label: text_17
text: Doherty leads a Harborwomen team, ranked No. 1 in the Globe’s Top 20, that has eyes on its first title since 2011. They’re off to a 6-0-0 start, with Doherty scoring 14 goals.

label: text_18
text: “She could probably go out here in some ofthese games and score 17 goals,” third-year Hing-ham coach Courtney Turner said. “But she’slooking for her teammates after the first one ortwo. I think that says more about her characterthan her scoring.”

label: text_19
text: Doherty burst onto the scene as a freshman, then exploded for 48 goals and 28 assists as a sophomore. After another 36 points a year ago and 17 to start the new season, she’s at 190 for

label: text_20
text: her career. Of those, 126 are goals — the 122nd of which set the Hingham record on Christ-mas Eve, assisted by her sister.

label: text_21
text: It’s easy to see the talent Do-herty possesses. She can take out defenders with her stick-handling and snipe a corner like clockwork.

label: text_22
text: But it’s her work ethic and drive to be better that have got-ten her here. Monday after-noon, she takes the ice more than 30 minutes before Hing-ham’s practice begins, getting extra work in with fellow cap-tain Addy Garrity.

label: text_23
text: “She puts in a lot of work be-hind the scenes that allows her to be a goal scorer,” Turner said. “She also just goes to the gym all the time. Her shot is a testa-ment to how much work she puts in at the gym.”

label: text_24
text: With her talent, Doherty could have easily taken the prep school route. But in sticking with the Harborwomen, she displayed that talent and hard work — not the school on your

label: text_25
text: sweater — make a college career possible.

label: text_26
text: “My first year here, we had the prep school discussion,” Turner said. “She wanted to stay here. I’m very happy she did, and I know she’ll have these friends for life.”

label: text_27
text: Doherty made a switch at the club level this year, moving to the Massachusetts Spitfires — ranked as one of the top programs not just in the state, but in the country. The move was all Do-herty’s doing — she reached out to coach Joe Hulbig to set up an opportunity, and even though the Spitfires had a full roster, she impressed enough to make the team. At their first tourna-ment of the year over Labor Day weekend, Hul-big said every college coach he talked to wanted to know about her.

label: text_28
text: Of the 19 players on the roster, she’s the only one at an MIAA program. Despite this, she fin-ished the fall season as the team’s top scorer with nine goals.

label: text_29
text: “She’s a rare athlete that has a natural ability to keep focus and discipline,” Hulbig said. “She wants it, and that’s what’s been able to make her successful.

label: text_30
text: “Someday, she’s going to look back at this and say, ’I’m glad I finished it out at Hingham,’ be-cause it’s a pretty special thing that she’s doing.”

label: text_31
text: Doherty committed to Holy Cross in Septem-ber and will join up with the Crusaders in fall 2026 to play for coach Katie Lachapelle at an up-and-coming program in Hockey East. She’ll join Spitfires teammate Violet Carroll (Williston Northampton) in Worcester. (She’s still undecid-ed where she will skate next season.)

label: text_32
text: “I fell in love with the school itself, which I think is bigger than the hockey part,” Dohertysaid. “When the hockey part fell into place, itwas just a perfect fit.”

label: text_33
text: That’s all in the future — at the moment, the 5-foot-6-inch sniger is focused on enjoying time with her friends in her hometown.

label: text_34
text: “I really just want to take in these last few months,” Doherty said. “Playing with my sister, all the seniors I won’t get to play with again, and all these girls. I just want to have fun and enjoy it.”

label: text_35
text: After years of preaching a defense-first mentality, King Philip coach Ken Assad is finally seeing his vision come to fruition.

label: text_36
text: Since dropping their season opener to Smith-field (R.I.), the Warriors have won five in a row, and they have given up one goal or less in four of the five victories.

label: text_40
text: King Philip’s new identity is led by sophomore Calleigh Bra-dy, junior Grace Leehan-Allen, and freshman Laney O’Shea on the blue line, and junior net-minder Kiki Lynch, who has al-lowed just six goals through six games.

label: text_41
text: After winning three consec-utive games by one-goal mar-gins, the Warriors secured their most impressive victory to date in a 3-0 win over No. 20 Canton on Saturday.

label: text_42
text: “It’s tribute to all the back-checkers, defenders, goaltend-ing, you name it, they’re all just coming together and playing as one,” Assad said. “It’s a differ-ent brand of hockey that they’re putting out this year.”

label: text_43
text: Canton got off to a 3-0-1 start under first-year coach Marissa Massaro, prior to dropping games this week to King Phillip and Notre Dame (Hingham).

label: text_44
text: One key weapon for the Bulldogs is sophomore forward Lauren Raffetto – who, when

label: text_45
text: she is not playing top-line minutes for the girls’ hockey team, is one of the state’s best cross-coun-try runners.

label: text_46
text: Raffetto finished 13th in the MIAA Division 2 Meet of Champions race in November, and she also owns Canton’s 5K school record time by 45 seconds.

label: text_47
text: Raffetto scored a goal in Canton’s 3-1 victory over No. 12 Nauset on Thursday, and her cross-country skill-set has proven to be an asset.

label: text_48
text: “Her endurance is incredible. She can play as many minutes as I possibly need,” Massaro said. “I think at one point [against Nauset], she played three minutes straight and got off the ice and wasn’t tired. She’s skilled and she’s aggressive in the best way possible, and she can go and go and never worry about running out of steam.”

text: G5

label: vision_footnote_04
text: Desnuda Cocina & Bar (above) and Russ & Mimi’s (right) are among the many exciting restaurants arriving on the scene.

label: doc_title_05
text: 10 new restaurants to try in the new year

label: vision_footnote_09
text: MICHAEL DISKIN

label: vision_footnote_10
text: JONATHAN WIGGS/GLOBE STAFF

label: text_11
text: ▶RESTAURANTS

label: text_12
text: Continued from Page G1

label: text_13
text: park belly bao buns and tacos, miso eggplant, and grilled steak with chimi-churri sauce. Chef Jesus Preciado’s menu draws from Asia and Latin Amer-ica (including his native Colombia). On the cocktail list, find drinks like Beet the Heat (made with spicy pisco and beet syrup) and Amarillo Passion (in which tequila meets yuzu liqueur, passion fruit syrup, and the aji amarillo chile).

label: text_14
text: 647 Tremont St., South End, Boston, 617-286-2333, www.desnudacoci-na.com. Smaller plates $6-$18, larger plates $18-$32, cocktails $14-$17.

label: text_15
text: Kaia

label: text_16
text: The latest from Xenia Greek Hospi-tality, which brought us Bar Vlaha, Kra-si, and more. This time, culinary direc-tor Brendan Pelley and team whisk din-ers to the Aegean (with a South End mind-set) via dishes like sea bream cru-do with fermented squash broth; barley toasts with beets, pears, and vegan feta; black truffle spanakopita; and grilled whole fish. The wine list is devoted sole-ly to selections from the Aegean and Eastern Mediterranean islands.

label: text_17
text: 370 Harrison Ave., South End, Bos-ton, 617-514-0700, www.kaiasouth-end.com. Dishes $16-$44.

label: paragraph_title_18
text: Masons Steakhouse

label: text_19
text: Here’s what happens when a group of powerhouse South Shore culinary pros (including Jimmy Liang of JP Fuji Group and Kevin Long of Tosca) join forces. This swank Quincy steakhouse is located in a former Masonic temple and serves up lobster bisque, oysters Rocke-feller, pappardelle bolognese, salmon with spiced cauliflower — and, of course, beautiful steaks. The also-beau-tiful, creative desserts are from pastry chef and Masons co-owner Robert Gon-zalez, who is behind Quincy’s Niveaux Pâtisserie. In a landscape (increasingly) stocked with steakhouses, it is nice to see a new one open with local owner-ship.

label: text_20
text: 1170 Hancock St., Quincy, 617-689-8818, www.masonsteakhouse.com.Ap-petizers $14-$32, entrees $29-$45, steaks $52-$160, sides $6-$14, desserts$12-$19.

label: paragraph_title_21
text: McGonagle’s Pub

label: text_22
text: If you appreciate the Dubliner, bringing excellent fish and chips and Irish hospitality to downtown Boston, you will likely feel the same about McG-onagle’s in Dorchester. Pigs in a blanket made with sausage from Adams Village

label: text_23
text: Butcher Shop, smoky seafood chowder with Irish soda bread, shepherd’s pie, bangers and mash, and other pub favorites are here, along with wood-fired pizza, brunch (yes, full Irish breakfast), and festive cocktails. Or just drop in for live music and a proper pint of Guin-ness.

label: text_24
text: 367 Neponset Ave., Dorchester, 617-514-4689, www.mcgonagles.com. Appe-tizers $8-$16, pizza $18-$19, entrees$18-$34.

label: paragraph_title_25
text: Mikiya Wagyu Shabu House

label: text_26
text: If you’re starving, cold, and enjoy wagyu beef, Mikiya is calling you. This Chinatown restaurant serves all-you-can-eat wagyu hot pot at a variety of price points; you have 90 minutes to cook a variety of cuts in the broths of your choosing, while eating specialty dishes such as sweet shrimp sashimi and wagyu bone marrow, plus fruit and ice cream for dessert. Mikiya is a project from Chubby Group, whose Kevin Liu is also behind Matsunori Handroll Bar.

label: text_27
text: Wagyu sets $45-$98 (less with annu-al membership; free or half-price for kids).

label: paragraph_title_28
text: Russ & Mimi's

label: text_29
text: Named for the parents of owner Kel-ly Walsh (Sweet Cheeks, Tiger Mama), this Roslindale market offers wine (it’s in the former Solera space), olive oil, hot sauce, and other must-haves. But it’s the food that has the neighborhood most

label: text_30
text: excited. Start the morning with egg wraps, overnight oats, cheesy grits, and cumin-spiced black beans with fried egg, salsa, and avocado; then segue into the “Cubano, veggie grinder, muffuletta, charred broccoli Caesar” part of the day. Chef Stephen Marcaurelle (the Nautilus Pier 4, Tres Gatos) helped design the menu.

label: text_31
text: 16 Birch St., Roslindale, 617-833-6950, www.russandmimis.com. Dishes

label: paragraph_title_32
text: Soul on Shawmut

label: text_33
text: Roxbury-raised chef Aadam Abdul-Musawwir began serving prepared meals and pop-up dinners as Aadam’s Halal Meals. Now, he and two siblings have opened Soul on Shawmut to feed their community. Lightly updated soul food classics are on the menu, along with Buffalo chicken egg rolls, grilled cheese burgers, and more. Fried chick-en with Old Bay honey, smoked mac and cheese, slow-cooked collard greens with sauteed cabbage, sweet potato cheesecake, and hibiscus watermelon juice sounds pretty unbeatable for din-ner tonight.

label: text_34
text: 722A Shawmut Ave., Roabury, 617-238-7525, www.soulonshawmut.com.Sandwiches $10-$18, fried chicken$7-$18, sides $5, desserts $3-$6.

label: paragraph_title_35
text: Standard Italian

label: text_36
text: Where others fail, there is Italian food. Standard Italian, in the Eastern Standard complex looming over Fen-way, replaces the former All That Fish + Oyster, and it’s a smart move. Lasagna bolognese, porchetta, and espresso martinis could just get us all through the winter. Culinary director Brian Rae is in his element, having previously worked at Coppa, Faccia a Faccia, and Rialto.

label: text_37
text: 771 Beacon St., Fenway, Boston, 857-305-3095, www.standarditalian.com.Appetizers $5-$20, entrees $28-$42, des-serts $9-$12.

label: paragraph_title_38
text: Zurito

label: text_39
text: It’s named for the small glass of beer that often accompanies pintxos, the Basque take on tapas, and this Beacon Hill restaurant serves up plenty: Gildas, skewers of anchovies, peppers, and ol-ives; griddled shrimp with garlic and chile oil; mini croissants stuffed with ja-mon iberico; squid ink risotto. Cocktails such as the sherry-based Perfect Bam-boo and fizzy glasses of tzakolina are perfect accompaniments. Zurito, locat-ed in the longtime Bin 26 space, is run by chef Jamie Bissonnette, Babak Bina, and Andy Cartin of BCB3 Hospitality, al-so behind Somaek, Temple Records, and Sushi @ Temple Records.

label: text_40
text: 26 Charles St., Beacon Hill, Boston,857-305-3177, www.zuritoboston.com.Pintxos $4.50-$12, raciones $9-$19,platos especiales $17-$125.

text: Restaurants continue to innovate in mocktail realm

label: text_44
text: ▶ MOCKTAILS

label: text_45
text: Continued from Page G1

label: text_46
text: there are a plethora of base op-tions that can really make a non-alcoholic drink look and taste nearly identical to an alcoholic one,” says Joel Atlas, a mixologist at the Avery Bar at the Ritz-Carl-ton, Boston. “The bloom of op-tions has really picked up in the last year and a half to two years.”

label: text_47
text: “[Mocktails] are certainly marketed more in January, but the truth of it all is that the non-alcoholic or low-ABV consumer is sustaining through much of the year,” says Nick Moniz, gen-eral manager of Banners Kitch-en and Tap and Hub Hall.

label: text_48
text: “For so long, a mocktail was limited to just a soda water and cranberry, or a sugar bomb of juices made with whatever was lying around behind the bar. Consumers wanted and de-served more than that.”

label: text_49
text: In that spirit − or lack there-of − here are 12 mocktail desti-nations to try every month of the year.

label: paragraph_title_50
text: Abe & Louie's

label: text_51
text: The storied steakhouse offers a $14 mocktail menu. Their New Year, New Spritz combines zero-proof sparkling Cava with non-alcoholic tequila, cucumber, lime, and mint for a spa-like pour. Good for: expense-account dining. 793 Boylston St., Boston, 617-536-6300

label: paragraph_title_52
text: Alcove

label: text_53
text: In the West End, cozy Alcove does an $11 mocktail menu with unusual offerings like Papi’s Punch, with grilled pineapple syrup and Athletic Free Wave nonalcoholic IPA, or a Queen’s Bee, made with the herbaceous nonalcoholic spirit Garden 108 and honey. Good for: T.D. Gar-den pre-game hangouts. 50 Love-joy Wharf, Boston, 617-248-0050

label: paragraph_title_54
text: Avery Bar at the Ritz-Carlton,Boston

label: text_55
text: This might be one of Boston’smost classic of cocktail refuges,but it also caters to modern mo-res. A nonalcoholic Old-Fash-

label: text_57

label: text_58
text: Baleia

label: text_59
text: This stylish new Portuguese restaurant in the South End, from the team behind Gufo and SRV, welcomes a cosmopolitan crowd eager to experiment with nonalcoholic delights. Try the Tropical Amargo, an aperitif made with coconut-chai, orange, lime, pineapple, and coffee, plus spirit-free Campari. Good for: date night. 264 East Berkeley St., Boston, 617-505-3243

label: paragraph_title_60
text: Bistro du Midi

label: text_61
text: This French restaurant enjoys a scenic perch overlooking the

label: vision_footnote_62
text: Above: Warming mocktailsat Capo in South Boston.Left: A cosmopolitan atBistro du Midi.

label: text_63
text: Public Garden, and it serves farmore than wine. A $10 mocktailmenu has spins on classics like ti-ki punch, a cosmopolitan, and aspicy citrus mule. Good for: din-ner with the parents. 272 Boyl-ston St., Boston, 617-279-8000

label: text_64
text: Capo

label: text_65
text: This South Boston red-sauce lair might seem like the type of spot to throw back icy martinis (they do host Sinatra Sundays, after all) paired with big plates of rigatoni Bolognese, but they also have warming $9 mocktails, like the Far From the Tree, with toasty apple cider, cardamom, allspice, thyme, and egg whites. In addition to catering to non-drinkers, they accommodate a range of palates, with gluten-free pasta on request. Good for: a night out with a group. 443 West Broadway, Boston, 617-993-8080

label: paragraph_title_66
text: Hunter's

label: text_67
text: This is your spot for biscuits, fried chicken, mac-and-cheese ... in other words, resolution-breaking meals. That said: This dark, cozy bar and kitchen also pays attention to mocktails, which are a relative steal at $6. Wash down your honey-butter,

label: text_68
text: bacon-topped cornbread with refreshing house-made water-melon juice and soda. Good for: comfort food. 110 Dorchester St, Boston, 617-221-4200

label: paragraph_title_69
text: La Padrona

label: text_70
text: Stylish, swanky, and with a stellar chef attached (Jody Ad-ams), this Italian destination in-side Raffles Boston is the uti-mate in special-occasion dining: The silken tagliatelle alone is worth the trip up that grand staircase. Sure, there’s also an ex-tensive martini menu, but spirit-free drinks also get proper due. A nonalcoholic tangerine marga-rita with spirit-free tequila and lime is worth toasting. Not quite ready to abstain? There’s also an extensive low-ABV list featuring treats like a Lambrusco Cobbler, made with black current and berries. Good for: a celebratory splurge. 38 Trinity Place, Boston, 617-221-4

label: paragraph_title_71
text: Midnight Morning

label: text_72
text: This cheery Roslindale bistrospecializes in comfort food: sausage dip, mushroom-and-cream-cheese wontons, burgers, andfried pickles. It makes nondrink-ers feel comfy, too, with a nic $12 selection of zero-proofdrinks: The Regret Nothing,with nonalcoholic Ritual Prooftequila, jalapeno, and lime, istrue to its name. Good for: a laid-back weeknight dinner. 14 BirchSt., Roslindale, 617-390-5830

label: paragraph_title_73
text: Trina’s Starlite Lounge

label: text_74
text: This industry hangout takes dive-bar food to another level — they pioneered dressed-up tater tots and mac-and-cheese before it was fashionable. Here, $5 cans of Miller High Life share real es-tate with cheeky mocktails like the Phony Negroni, a nonalco-holic version of the classic, and Island Life, Baby, made with a booze-free, floral Fluère Botanic Blend. Good for: dive-bar-dining without the buzz. 3 Beacon St., Somerville, 617-576-0006

Beverage director Jose Luis Betancur also has a fondness for tart Italian so-das like Chinotto or Stappi Gas-sosa.
